306                                              16 The Jacobs–de Leeuw–Glicksberg Decomposition
                    
                 clσ T n f : n ∈ N0            is weakly compact for each f ∈ E.

Then T is certainly power-bounded. By 3)
                 
            conv T n f : n ∈ N0   is weakly compact for each f ∈ E.

In particular, for each f ∈ E the sequence (An [T ] f )n∈N of Cesàro means has a weak
cluster point, whence by Proposition 8.18 it actually converges in norm. To sum up,
we have shown that if T generates a relatively weakly compact semigroup, then T
is mean ergodic.
The converse statement fails to hold. In fact, Example 8.27 exhibits a multiplication
operator T on c, the space of convergent sequences, such that T is mean ergodic but
T 2 is not. However, T 2 generates a relatively weakly compact semigroup as soon
as T does so. Thus T is mean ergodic but does not generate a relatively weakly
compact semigroup.

    We close this section with a classical result. If S is a semigroup and a ∈ S, then as
in the group case we denote by La and Ra the left and the right rotation by a defined
as (La f )(x) = f (ax) and (Ra f )(x) = f (xa) for f : S → C and x ∈ S.

Theorem 16.18. Let S be a compact semitopological semigroup. Then the semi-
group of left rotations {La : a ∈ S} is a weakly compact semigroup of operators on
C(S).

Proof. By Lemma 16.16 we only have to check that for fixed f ∈ C(S) the orbit
M := {La f : a ∈ S} is weakly compact in C(S). By Grothendieck’s Theorem G.5,
this is equivalent to M being compact in Cp (S), the space C(S) endowed with the
pointwise topology. But by separate continuity of the multiplication of S, the map-
ping
                             S → Cp (S),     a 7→ La f
is continuous. Since S is compact, its image is compact.



16.3 The Jacobs–de Leeuw–Glicksberg Decomposition

Let E be a Banach space and let T ⊆ L (E) be a semigroup of operators on E. Then

                                             S := clw (T ),

the weak operator closure of T , is a semitopological semigroup. We call the semi-
group T Jacobs–de Leeuw–Glicksberg admissible (or briefly: JdLG-admissible)
if S is weakly compact and contains a unique minimal idempotent, i.e., satisfies the
equivalent conditions of Theorem 16.5. (Note that by Theorem 16.3 every weakly
compact operator semigroup contains at least one minimal idempotent.)
The following gives a list of important examples.


Published: Graduate Text in Mathematics, vol. 272, Springer-Verlag, 2015.
16.3 The Jacobs–de Leeuw–Glicksberg Decomposition                                    307

Theorem 16.19. Let E be a Banach space and T ⊆ Lw (E) a semigroup of opera-
tors on E. Then T is JdLG-admissible in the following cases:
   1) T is Abelian and relatively weakly compact.
   2) E is a Hilbert space and T consists of contractions.
   3) E = L1 (X), X a probability space, and T ⊆ M(X), i.e., T consists of
      Markov operators.
Proof. The case 1) was already mentioned in Theorem 16.5. (Note that by Exercise
14.2 the closure S of T is Abelian, too.) The case 3) can be reduced to 2) via
Corollary 16.14. To prove 2) suppose that P and Q are minimal idempotents in
S = clw (T ). Then P and Q are contractive hence orthogonal projections (Theorem
D.21). Since S Q is a minimal left ideal (Lemma 16.1) and S PQ is a left ideal
contained in S Q, it follows that these left ideals are identical. Hence, there is an
operator S ∈ S such that SPQ = QQ = Q. Now let f ∈ H be arbitrary. Since S and
P are contractions, it follows that

                              kQ f k = kSPQ f k ≤ kPQ f k ≤ kQ f k .

So kPQ f k = kQ f k, and since P is an orthogonal projection, by Corollary D.22
we obtain PQ f = Q f . Since f ∈ H was arbitrary, we conclude that PQ = Q, i.e.,
ran(Q) ⊆ ran(P). By symmetry ran(P) = ran(Q), and since orthogonal projections
are uniquely determined by their range, it follows that P = Q.
   With a little more effort one can show the following.
Theorem 16.20. If E and its dual space E 0 both are strictly convex, then every rel-
atively weakly compact semigroup of contractions on E is JdLG-admissible.

Sketch of proof. Recall that a Banach space E is strictly convex if k f k = kgk = 1
and f 6= g implies that k f + gk < 2. If P is a contractive projection on a strictly con-
vex space E, then it has the property in Corollary D.22.a), see Exercise 11. Hence,
by the same reasoning as in the proof above we conclude that PQ = Q. By taking
right ideals in place of left ideals, we find an operator T ∈ S such that PQT = P,
and taking adjoints yields P0 = T 0 Q0 P0 . If E 0 is also strictly convex, it follows as
before that P0 = Q0 P0 , i.e., P = PQ = Q.
The theorem is applicable to spaces Lp (X) with 1 < p < ∞, since these are strictly
convex and (Lp )0 = Lq with 1p + q1 = 1. Note that these spaces are reflexive, hence
contraction semigroups are automatically relatively weakly compact.
Corollary 16.21. Every semigroup of contractions on a space Lp (X), X some mea-
sure space and 1 < p < ∞, is JdLG-admissible.
Remark 16.22. Theorem 16.20 is due to de Leeuw and Glicksberg (1961), Cor.
4.14. There one can find even a characterization of JdLG-admissible semigroups
in terms of the amenability of their weak closures. See (Day 1957) and (Pater-
son 1988) for more about this notion.


Published: Graduate Text in Mathematics, vol. 272, Springer-Verlag, 2015.
308                                              16 The Jacobs–de Leeuw–Glicksberg Decomposition

The JdLG-Decomposition

As before, let E be a Banach space, let T ⊆ L (E) be a semigroup of operators and
let
                                  S = clw (T )
be its weak operator closure. In the following we shall suppose that T is JdLG-
admissible, i.e., S is weakly compact and contains a unique minimal idempotent
Q.
By Theorem 16.5, S has a unique nonempty minimal ideal

                              G := K(S ) = QS = S Q = QS Q,                              (16.2)

which is a group with unit element Q. Since Q2 = Q, Q is a projection and the space
E decomposes into a direct sum

       E = Erev (T ) ⊕ Eaws (T ) = ran(Q) ⊕ ker(Q) = ker(I − Q) ⊕ ran(I − Q),

called the Jacobs–de Leeuw–Glicksberg decomposition (JdLG-decomposition for
short) of E associated with T . This decomposition goes back to Jacobs (1956),
de Leeuw and Glicksberg (1959), (1961). The space Erev := Erev (S ) is called the
reversible part of E and its elements the reversible vectors; the space Eaws :=
Eaws (T ) is called the almost weakly stable part and its element the almost weakly
stable vectors. Both are closed subspaces of E. This terminology will become clear
shortly. Moreover, we shall see below that for T = TT = {T n : n ∈ N0 } consisting
of the iterates of one single operator T ∈ L (E), we have Eaws (T ) = Eaws (T ), as
introduced in Section 9.2.

Proposition 16.23. In the situation above, the minimal idempotent Q of S satisfies

                                   T Q = QT            for all T ∈ T .

In particular Erev and Eaws are invariant under S .

Proof. This is an immediate consequence of (v) in Theorem 16.5.

   By Proposition 16.23, we may restrict the operators from S to the invariant
subspaces Erev and Eaws and obtain
                                           
     Trev := T |Erev : T ∈ T ,     Srev := S|Erev : S ∈ S ⊆ L (Erev )
                                           
and Taws := T |Eaws : T ∈ T ,      Saws := S|Eaws : S ∈ S ⊆ L (Eaws ).

By Exercise 12, the restriction maps

                                  S 7→ S|Erev      and     S 7→ S|Eaws

are continuous for the weak operator topologies. Since S is compact and S =
clw (T ), it follows that


Published: Graduate Text in Mathematics, vol. 272, Springer-Verlag, 2015.
16.3 The Jacobs–de Leeuw–Glicksberg Decomposition                                  309

                         Srev = clw (Trev ) and             Saws = clw (Taws ).

The following theorem shows that a vector u ∈ E is reversible if and only if, when-
ever some vector v can be reached by the action of S starting from u, then one can
return to u again by the action of S . This explains the terminology.

Theorem 16.24. Let E = Erev ⊕ Eaws be the JdLG-decomposition of a Banach space
E with respect to a JdLG-admissible semigroup T ⊆ L (E) with weak closure S :=
clw (T ) and minimal idempotent Q in S . Then the following assertions hold:
    a) The reversible part Erev is given by
                            
                     Erev = u ∈ E : v ∈ clσ (T u) ⇒ u ∈ clσ (T v)
                            
                          = u∈E : v∈Su ⇒ u∈Sv .

   b) The minimal ideal G := K(S ) is a compact topological group with neutral
      element Q, the strong and the weak operator topologies coincide on G , and
      the restriction map
                              G → Srev ,     S 7→ S|Erev
         is a topological isomorphism of compact groups.

Proof. a) Recall that Q acts as the identity on Erev = ran(Q). If u ∈ Erev , then S u =
S Qu = G u. Hence if v ∈ S u, then there is R ∈ G with v = Ru. Since G is a group,
there is S ∈ G with SR = Q. Hence, u = Qu = SRu = Sv ∈ S v. Conversely, if u ∈ E
is such that there is S ∈ S with SQu = u, then u = SQu = QSu ∈ ran(Q).
b) For the special case when E is a Hilbert space and T is a semigroup of contrac-
tions, this is Theorem 16.12. In the case that E = L1 (X), X some probability space,
and T ⊆ M(X) is semigroup of Markov operators, it is Corollary 16.15.
In the general case, it follows from Ellis’ Theorem 16.6 that G is a compact group.
The assertion about the topological isomorphism is then evident. That the strong
and the weak operator topologies coincide on G follows from Theorem 15.6.

Example 16.25 (Contraction Semigroups on Hilbert Spaces). Let H be a Hilbert
space and let T ⊆ L (H) be a semigroup of contractions. Then T is JdLG-
admissible by Theorem 16.19. The minimal idempotent Q ∈ S is a contraction,
hence self-adjoint, and the corresponding JdLG-decomposition

                                            H = Hrev ⊕ Haws

is an orthogonal decomposition. On Hrev the semigroup S := clw (T ) restricts to
a compact group of unitary operators. Because Q = Q∗ , the projection Q is also
an idempotent in the adjoint semigroup S ∗ = {S∗ : S ∈ S }. Since taking adjoints
is a homeomorphism and (up to order) a semigroup homomorphism on the set of
all contractions, Q is also the minimal idempotent in S ∗ . Consequently, the JdlG-
decompositions for T and T ∗ coincide in this case.



Published: Graduate Text in Mathematics, vol. 272, Springer-Verlag, 2015.
310                                              16 The Jacobs–de Leeuw–Glicksberg Decomposition

Remark 16.26 (Mean Ergodic Semigroups). We claim that JdLG-admissible

Theorem 16.20, this yields an alternative proof of Theorem 8.34.
To establish the claim, suppose that T ⊆ L (X) is a JdLG-admissible semigroup
with weak closure S = clw (T ), minimal ideal G and minimal idempotent Q. Let,
as in Example 15.4,                       Z

                                                        G
(where m is the Haar probability measure on G ) be the mean ergodic projection
associated with G . Then, for every T ∈ T ,

            T P = T (QP) = (T Q)P = P and                    PT = (PQ)T = P(QT ) = P

since QT, T Q ∈ G . Moreover, for each u ∈ E,
                                                 
      Pu ∈ conv Su : S ∈ G ⊆ conv Su : S ∈ S = conv Tu : T ∈ T .

This shows that T is mean ergodic as claimed.


The Almost Weakly Stable Part

We now investigate the two parts of the JdLG-decomposition separately. Let us first
deal with the almost weakly stable part.
Proposition 16.27. Let E = Erev ⊕ Eaws be the JdLG-decomposition of a Banach
space E with respect to a JdLG-admissible semigroup T ⊆ L (E) with weak closure
S := clw (T ). Then the following assertions hold:
    a) Taws is a JdLG-admissible semigroup on Eaws with weak operator closure
       Saws .
   b) The minimal idempotent of Saws is the zero operator 0 ∈ Saws , and its mini-
      mal ideal is K(Saws ) = {0}.
    c) The elements of Eaws are characterized by
                                
        u ∈ Eaws ⇐⇒ 0 ∈ clσ Tu : T ∈ T           ⇐⇒ Su = 0                   for some S ∈ S .

Proof. Let Q be the minimal idempotent of S . Then Q restricts to 0 on Eaws , and
hence a) and b) are evident.
For c), note first that for each u ∈ E the mapping T 7→ Tu is continuous from Lw (E)
to (E, σ (E, E 0 )). Since S = clw (T ) is compact, one has clσ (T u) = (clw T )u =
S u. This proves the second equivalence in c).
If u ∈ Eaws = ker(Q), then it follows immediately that 0 = Qu ∈ S u. Conversely,
suppose that Su = 0 for some S ∈ S . Since QS ∈ G = K(S ) and G is a group with
unit element Q, there is R ∈ G such that RQS = Q. So, Qu = RQSu = 0, whence
u ∈ Eaws follows.


Published: Graduate Text in Mathematics, vol. 272, Springer-Verlag, 2015.
16.3 The Jacobs–de Leeuw–Glicksberg Decomposition                                     311

   A JdLG-admissible semigroup T on a Banach space E is called almost weakly
stable if E = Eaws . Equivalently, T is almost weakly stable if 0 is in the weak
closure of each orbit {Tu : T ∈ T }, u ∈ E.
Remark 16.28. A semigroup T can be almost weakly stable even if it is already a
group of unitary operators. Indeed, take H := `2 (Z) and T the (right or left) shift.
Then T is a unitary operator and hence T := {T n : n ∈ Z} is a relatively weakly
compact group of unitary operators. But T n f → 0 weakly for every f ∈ H, whence
H = Haws and Hrev = {0}.


The Reversible Part

Let us now look at the reversible part. We start with a characterization that is often
useful.
Proposition 16.29. Let T be a JdLG-admissible semigroup of bounded linear op-
erators on a Banach space E. Then
               
         Eaws ∩ x ∈ E : T x relatively compact and inf kT xk > 0 = /0.
                                                                       T ∈T

In particular, if infT ∈T kTyk > 0 for every y 6= 0 such that T y is relatively compact
in E, then Erev = {x ∈ E : T x is relatively compact in E}.
Proof. Let Q be the minimal idempotent of S := clw T , i.e., the projection onto
Erev along Eaws . Let x ∈ Eaws such that T x is relatively compact. Then the weak
closure of T x coincides with the norm closure. But then 0 = Qx ∈ T x and hence
0 = infT ∈T kT xk.
In the second assertion, the inclusion “⊆” follows from Theorem 16.24.b). For the
converse, let x ∈ E such that T x is relatively compact and define y := x − Qx ∈ Eaws .
Then T y is relatively compact as well, hence by the first assertion infT ∈T kTyk = 0.
But then, by hypothesis, y = 0, i.e., x = Qx ∈ Erev .
Corollary 16.30. Let T be a JdLG-admissible semigroup of linear isometries on a
Banach space E. Then Erev = {x ∈ E : T x is relatively compact in E}.
    Similar to group representations (see Chapter 15), let us call a tuple (e j )nj=1 of
vectors of E a (finite) unitary system for a semigroup T ⊆ L (E) if (e1 , . . . , en )
is linearly independent, F := lin{e1 , . . . , en } is T -invariant, and the corresponding
matrix representation χ of T on F defined by
                                   n
                         Tei = ∑ χi j (T )e j           (i = 1, . . . , n, T ∈ T )
                                  j=1

satisfies χ(T ) ∈ U(n) for each T ∈ T . Furthermore, a unitary system (e j )nj=1 for
T is called irreducible if F does not have nontrivial subspaces invariant under the
action of T .


Published: Graduate Text in Mathematics, vol. 272, Springer-Verlag, 2015.
312                                              16 The Jacobs–de Leeuw–Glicksberg Decomposition

Theorem 16.31 (Jacobs, de Leeuw, Glicksberg). Let E = Erev ⊕Eaws be the JdLG-
decomposition of a Banach space E with respect to a JdLG-admissible semigroup
T ⊆ L (E). Then
              
    Erev = lin u : (e j ) j (irred.) unitary system for T and u = e j for some j .

Proof. We use the previous terminology, i.e., S = clw (T ) is the weak operator
closure of T , Q the minimal idempotent, Erev = ran(Q) and G := S Q = QS .
Let B := (e1 , . . . , en ) be some unitary system for T and denote by F :=
lin{e1 , . . . , en } the generated subspace. As F is closed and invariant under T , it must
be invariant under S as well. Let χ be the matrix representation of S on F with re-
spect to the basis B. Then χ is continuous and a homomorphism of semigroups. By
hypothesis, χ(T ) ⊆ U(n), and since the latter is closed in L (Cn ), χ(S) ∈ U(n) for
all S ∈ S . In particular, χ(Q) ∈ U(n), and since Q is an idempotent, χ(Q) = In , the
n × n identity matrix. This means that Q acts as the identity on F, whence F ⊆ Erev .
For the converse we first note that the compact group G acts continuously on Erev .
Hence, by Theorem 15.14, Erev is the closed linear span of all irreducible unitary
systems for this representation. But it is clear that each unitary system (e j )nj=1 in
Erev for G is a unitary system for T , since T = T Q on Erev for every T ∈ T .
Further, if it is irreducible for the G -action, then it is irreducible for the T -action as
well since G ⊆ clw (T ).
We refer to Exercise 16 for a converse to Theorem 16.31. In the case of Abelian
semigroups, employing Corollary 15.18 we obtain the following information about
the reversible part.
Corollary 16.32. Let E be a Banach space, and let T ⊆ L (E) be an Abelian rela-
tively weakly compact semigroup. Then
                         
               Erev = lin u ∈ E : ∀ T ∈ T ∃ λ ∈ T with Tu = λ u .



16.4 Cyclic Semigroups of Operators

In the following we investigate more closely the special case of the semigroup
                                   
                              TT = I, T, T 2 , T 3 , . . .

generated by a single operator T ∈ L (E). We suppose that this semigroup is rela-
tively weakly compact. (Recall that this is automatic if T is power-bounded and E
is reflexive, or if T is a Markov operator on some L1 (X).) Then ST := clw (TT ) is
Abelian, hence TT is JdLG-admissible, and we can form the JdLG-decomposition

                            E = Erev ⊕ Eaws = Erev (TT ) ⊕ Eaws (TT )

associated with TT .

16.4 Cyclic Semigroups of Operators                                                      313

Theorem 16.33. Let T ∈ L (E) generate a relatively weakly compact semigroup TT
with associated JdLG-decomposition E = Erev ⊕Eaws . Then the following assertions
hold:
    a) Erev is spanned by the eigenvectors associated with unimodular eigenvalues
       of T , i.e.,
                                                            [
              Erev = lin u ∈ E : ∃ λ ∈ T with Tu = λ u = lin    ker(λ I − T ).
                                                                             λ ∈T

         If T is an isometry then
                           
                     Erev = u ∈ E : {T n u : n ≥ 0} is relatively compact .

   b) T is mean ergodic, fix(T ) ⊆ Erev                 and      Eaws ⊆ ran(I − T ).
    c) Eaws = ran(I − T )            if and only if σp (T ) ∩ T ⊆ {1}.
   d) E = Eaws            if and only if σp (T ) ∩ T = /0.

Proof. a) The first assertion follows from Corollary 16.32 since if Tu = λ u, then
T n u = λ n u for all n ∈ N0 . The second follows from Corollary 16.30.
b) The inclusion fix(T ) ⊆ Erev follows from a), but is self-evident since the projec-

For the second inclusion let u ∈ Eaws , i.e., 0 ∈ clσ {T n u : n ∈ N0 }. But then 0 ∈

To prove mean ergodicity it suffices to show that T is mean ergodic on Erev , and
this follows from a). Alternatively one can argue that for given f ∈ E the orbit
{ f , T f , T 2 f , . . . } is relatively weakly compact, and the same is true for the convex
hull, by Kreı̌n’s Theorem C.11.
c) follows from b) and a), and d) follows from a) directly.

    It follows that on Erev the action of T embeds into a faithful representation of
the compact monothetic group G := ST |Erev . By Exercise 15.9, the dual group G∗
is generated by those characters χ such that Pχ 6= 0, i.e., such that χ(T ) ∈ σp (T ) is
an eigenvalue of T .
   We look at a closer description of Eaws and thereby explain the term “almost
weakly stable”. Recall from Chapter 9, page 162, that a sequence (xn )n∈N in a topo-
logical space converges in density to x, in notation D-limn→∞ xn = x, if there is a
subsequence J ⊆ N with density d(J) = 1 such that limn∈J xn = x.

Theorem 16.34. Let T generate a relatively weakly compact semigroup TT on a

Remark 16.35. Theorem 16.34 states in particular that the almost weakly stable
subspace Eaws associated with TT coincides with Eaws (T ) from Section 9.2.
    We give another characterization of Erev in the case of a semigroup generated by
a single operator. A power-bounded operator T ∈ L (E) on a Banach space E is said
to have discrete spectrum if
                             
                      E = lin u ∈ E : ∃ λ ∈ T with Tu = λ u .

Theorem 16.36. For an operator T ∈ L (E) on a Banach space E the following
assertions are equivalent:
   (i) The operator T has discrete spectrum.
  (ii) The operator T generates a relatively weakly compact operator semigroup
       on E, and E = Erev (T ).
 (iii) The weak operator closure clw {T n : n ≥ 0} is a weakly/strongly compact
       group of invertible operators.
 (iv) The operator T is contained in a strongly compact subgroup G ⊆ L (E) of
      invertible operators.
  (v) {T n x : n ≥ 0} is relatively compact and infT ∈T kT xk > 0 for all 0 6= x ∈ E.
Proof. (i) ⇒ (ii): It is clear that the orbit {T n u : n ≥ 0} is relatively strongly (hence
weakly) compact whenever Tu = λ u, λ ∈ T. Therefore, by Lemma 16.16, if T
has discrete spectrum, then T generates a weakly compact operator semigroup on
E. By Theorem 16.33, the reversible part Erev (T ) is generated by the eigenvectors
corresponding to unimodular eigenvalues, hence coincides with E, by hypothesis.
(ii) ⇒ (iii): Let S := clw {T n : n ≥ 0}, which is an Abelian weakly compact oper-
ator semigroup. By hypothesis, E = Erev , i.e., the minimal idempotent in S is the
identity operator. Hence, S = K(S ) is a (weakly) compact topological group of
invertible operators.
(iii) ⇒ (iv): If clw {T n : n ≥ 0} is a weakly compact group of invertible operators,
then, by Theorem 16.24, the weak and strong operator topologies coincide on it.
(iv) ⇒ (v): This is immediate.
(v) ⇒ (i): If (v) holds, then (ii) follows from Proposition 16.29. But then (i) is im-
mediate from Theorem 16.33.

Contractions on Hilbert Spaces

Let T be a contraction on a Hilbert space. Then, by Example 16.25, the JdLG-
decomposition
                           H = Hrev (T ) ⊕ Haws (T )
is orthogonal. It is instructive to compare it with the Szőkefalvi-Nagy–Foiaş de-
composition H = Huni ⊕ Hcnu (Theorem D.27) into a unitary and a completely
nonunitary part. Clearly

                                 Hrev ⊆ Huni        and     Hcnu ⊆ Haws .

By Theorem 16.34, the vectors f ∈ Haws are characterized by the existence of a sub-
sequence (n j ) j∈N ⊆ N with T n j f → 0 weakly as j → ∞. On the other hand, vectors
 f ∈ Hcnu satisfy T n f → 0 weakly as n → ∞ (Theorem D.28). If T is an isometry
then the Szőkelfalvi-Nagy–Foiaş decomposition becomes T
                                                           the Wold decomposition
of H with respect to T . The unitary part is then Huni = n≥0 ran(T n ), see Theorem
D.29. We return to the relation between these two decompositions in Chapter 18.
   We close this chapter with a nice application of the JdLG-splitting theory to
Hilbert space contractions.

The Kronecker Factor and Systems with
Discrete Spectrum




   I want to know how God created this world. I am not interested in this or that phenomenon,
   in the spectrum of this or that element. I want to know His thoughts, the rest are details.
                                                                             Albert Einstein1

In this chapter we apply the splitting theory from Chapter 16 to semigroups of
Markov operators and, in particular, to the semigroup generated by the Koopman
operator of a dynamical system. In the ergodic case, the reversible part, the so-called
Kronecker factor, is described by the classical Halmos–von Neumann theorem from
1942 and becomes the first building block for a deeper structure theory of dynamical
systems. Its complement, the almost weakly stable part, relates to mixing properties
of dynamical systems. In the last section, the Kronecker factor is determined in a
couple of important examples.



17.1 Semigroups of Markov Operators and the Kronecker
     Factor

Let X be a probability space and let T ⊆ M(X) be a set of Markov operators. Then

                                      S := clw sgr(T )

is a weakly compact semigroup of Markov operators on E = L1 (X). Since
S is JdLG-admissible by Theorem 16.19, we obtain a corresponding JdLG-
decomposition
                    E = Erev ⊕ Eaws = ran(Q) ⊕ ker(Q),
where Q is the unique minimal idempotent in S .
   Since S consists of Markov operators, Q is a Markov projection commuting
with the operators from T , and hence Erev = ran(Q) is a strict T -factor of X, see

1 E. Salaman, A Talk with Einstein, The Listener 54 (1955), 370–371.




                                                                                             321
322                                    17 The Kronecker Factor and Systems with Discrete Spectrum

Theorem 13.29. This factor is called the Kronecker factor of T and denoted by

      Kro := Kro(X; T ) := reversible part in the JdLG-decomposition of L1 (X)
                                    with respect to T .

The group G := QS = S Q is compact, and

                                π : G → L (Kro),               πS := S|Kro

is a faithful continuous Markov representation. Hence, the results of Chapter 15
apply.
Example 17.1 (Fixed Factor). The Kronecker factor associated with the convex
semigroup conv(T ) coincides with the fixed factor of T , i.e.,
                                                                     \
                          Kro(X; conv(T )) = fix(T ) =                      fix(T ),

see Example 13.27 and Exercise 16.17. The corresponding Markov projection P2 =
P ∈ M(X) with ran(P) = fix(T ) is the mean ergodic projection associated with T ,
see also Remark 13.25. Clearly, fix(T ) ⊆ Kro(X; T ), and PQ = QP = P.
Example 17.2 (Markov Embeddings). If T is a semigroup of Markov embed-
dings on a probability space X, then
                            
              Kro(X; T ) = f ∈ L1 (X) : T f is relatively compact .

This follows from Corollary 16.30.
   From now on we suppose that T is a semigroup. By Theorem 16.31, Kro(X; T )
is generated by the finite unitary T -systems. Recall that such a system consists of
a sequence (e1 , . . . , en ) of vectors in E and a multiplicative mapping (=semigroup
representation)
                                         χ : T → U(n)
such that Tei = ∑nj=1 χ(T )i j e j . By analogy to eigenvalues and eigenvectors, we call
the tuple (e1 , . . . , en ) an eigensystem associated with χ.

Definition 17.4. Let A be a subalgebra of L∞ (X). A subspace F of L1 (X) is called

   In the situation from above, each T ∈ T acts on Kro(X; T ) as a Markov em-

states, in particular, that each space Eχ is a fix(T )-module.
We say that the semigroup T of Markov operators on L1 (X) is ergodic if fix(T ) =
C1. This is perfectly in coherence with the concept of ergodicity of measure-
preserving systems, cf. also Section 15.4. If T is ergodic and if (e1 , . . . , en ) is a
χ-eigensystem of T , then by Lemma 17.3 e = (∑nj=1 |e j |2 )1/2 is a constant func-
tion, hence each e j is contained in L∞ . Furthermore, the Kronecker factor Kro(X; T )
is an ergodic G -system, hence Corollary 15.28 applies.

Theorem 17.5. Let T be an ergodic semigroup of Markov operators on some prob-
ability space X. Then the action of S := clw T on Kro(X; T ) is equivalent to the
canonical rotation action of a compact group G on H\G for some closed subgroup
H of G.


Abelian Markov Semigroups

Now we suppose that the semigroup T is Abelian. Then one can employ Corollary
16.32. It states that to build up the Kronecker factor it suffices to consider one-
dimensional “unitary” systems, i.e., common eigenvectors of the operators T ∈ T
associated with unimodular eigenvalues. In the ergodic case one can apply Corollary
15.29 and obtain the following.


Published: Graduate Text in Mathematics, vol. 272, Springer-Verlag, 2015.
324                                    17 The Kronecker Factor and Systems with Discrete Spectrum

Theorem 17.6. Let T be an Abelian semigroup of Markov operators on a proba-
bility space X. Then its Kronecker factor is
                           
          Kro(X; T ) = lin u ∈ L∞ (X) : ∀ T ∈ T ∃ λ ∈ T with Tu = λ u .

If T is ergodic, then the action of S := clw (T ) on Kro(X; T ) is equivalent to the
canonical rotation action of a compact Abelian group G on itself.


The Kronecker Factor in Lp

Let T be a semigroup of Markov operators on a probability space X, and let 1 <
p < ∞. Denote by
                          
                    T p := T |Lp : T ∈ T ⊆ L (Lp (X))

the restricted semigroup. Then we can form its associated JdLG-decomposition of
Lp (X). As in the case p = 1 we denote

      Kro := Kro(X; T p ) := reversible part in the JdLG-decomposition of Lp (X)
                                    with respect to the semigroup T p .

Since the map T 7→ T |Lp is a homeomorphism and a semigroup isomorphism
(Proposition 13.6), the JdLG-theories for T and T p are identical. In particular, if Q
is the JdLG-projection of T onto Kro(T ), then Q|Lp is the JdLG-projection of T p
onto Kro(T p ). Since, trivially, ran(Q|Lp ) = ran(Q) ∩ Lp , we arrive at the following
useful fact.

Proposition 17.7. In the situation from above, Kro(X; T p ) = Kro(X; T ) ∩ Lp .

  Since Kro(X; T ) is a factor, Kro(X; T ) ∩ Lp is dense in Kro(X; T ), and hence
one can switch freely between the L1 -case and the Lp -case.



17.2 Dynamical Systems with Discrete Spectrum

Next, we confine our attention to semigroups TT = sgr{T } generated by one single
Markov operator T ∈ M(X), where the associated Kronecker factor is denoted by
Kro(X; T ) := Kro(X; TT ). If T := Tϕ is the Koopman operator on L1 (X) of a dy-
namical system (X; ϕ), then we also write Kro(X; ϕ) in place of Kro(T ) and call it
the Kronecker factor of (X; ϕ).
   Let us summarize what we know from the general theory of the previous section:
   1) The Kronecker factor Kro(X; T ) is a strict T -factor of L1 (X).
   2) T acts as a Markov isomorphism on Kro(X; T ).

   4) The space                                   [

   5) If T is the Koopman operator of a system (X; ϕ), then

The Kronecker factor Kro(X; T ) is certainly included in the invertible core of T , i.e.,
the largest factor of the system on which T is invertible, see Example 13.34. This
                   T
factor is given by n∈N ran(T n ) and it coincides (after restriction to the L2 -spaces)
with the unitary part of H in the Wold decomposition, cf. also Example 13.34 and
the paragraph on page 316 preceding Proposition 16.37.
Recall from Section 16.4 that a power-bounded operator T on a Banach space E
is said to have discrete spectrum if the linear span of eigenvectors associated with
unimodular eigenvalues of T is dense in E. A topological dynamical system (K; ϕ)
is said to have discrete spectrum if its associated Koopman operator Tϕ on C(K)
has discrete spectrum. Similarly, a measure-preserving system (X; ϕ) has discrete
spectrum if its associated Koopman operator Tϕ on L1 (X) has discrete spectrum.
We say that f , g ∈ L2 (X) correlate with each other if ( f |g) 6= 0.

Corollary 17.8. Let (X; ϕ) be a measure-preserving system with Koopman operator
Tϕ , and let 1 ≤ p < ∞. Then the following assertions are equivalent:
   (i) The system (X; ϕ) has discrete spectrum.
  (ii) The Koopman operator Tϕ has discrete spectrum on Lp (X).
 (iii) The Kronecker factor of (X; ϕ) is all of L1 (X).
 (iv) Each 0 6= f ∈ L2 (X) correlates with some bounded eigenfunction associated
      with an unimodular eigenvalue of Tϕ .

Proof. We write Tp for the restriction of Tϕ to Lp . The equivalences (i) ⇔ (ii) for
p = 1 and (i) ⇔ (iii) are clear. By Proposition 17.7, (iii) is equivalent to Kro(X; Tp ) =
Lp . By 3) above, bounded eigenfunctions generate Kro(X; T2 ), hence assertion (iv)
simply states that Kro(X; T2 )⊥ = {0}. This is equivalent to (ii) for p = 2.

Example 17.9. Let G be a compact Abelian group and let La be the Koopman op-
erator induced by the rotation by a ∈ G. Since every character χ ∈ G∗ is an eigen-
function of La corresponding to the eigenvalue χ(a) ∈ T and since lin G∗ is dense
in C(G) (Proposition 14.7), La has discrete spectrum on C(G). A fortiori, La has
discrete spectrum also on Lp (G) for every 1 ≤ p < ∞.

Example 17.10. Let T be the Koopman operator of an ergodic measure-preserving
system (X; ϕ) such that L1 (X) is not finite-dimensional. Then T is not mean ergodic
on L∞ by Proposition 12.28. A fortiori, T does not have discrete spectrum on L∞ .


Published: Graduate Text in Mathematics, vol. 272, Springer-Verlag, 2015.
326                                    17 The Kronecker Factor and Systems with Discrete Spectrum

In particular, the Koopman operator La of an irrational rotation (T; a) has discrete
spectrum on L2 but not on L∞ .

   Suppose now that (X; ϕ) is an ergodic measure-preserving system with discrete
spectrum. By the second part of Theorem 17.6, the system is Markov isomorphic
to a rotation system (G, m; a) for a compact Abelian group G with Haar measure m
and some element a ∈ G. As the rotation system must be ergodic, too, the group G
is monothetic with a being a generating element (Proposition 10.13 and Proposition
14.21). By Proposition 14.22, the dual G∗ of G is isomorphic to the subgroup
                                  
                            Γ := χ(a) : χ ∈ G∗ ⊆ T.

Under this isomorphism, by the Pontryagin duality theorem (Theorem 14.14), G ∼  =
Γ ∗ with a ∈ G corresponding to the canonical inclusion map Γ → T, χ 7→ χ(a).
Note that, by Proposition 14.24, Γ = σp (La ) is the point spectrum of the Koopman
operator. Hence, the rotation system (G, m; a) can be determined from the original
system (X; ϕ) in the following way:
   1) Form Γ := σp (Tϕ ), where Tϕ is the Koopman operator of (X; ϕ). Then Γ is
      a subgroup of T.
   2) Define G := Γ ∗ , the dual group of Γ . This is a compact Abelian group.
   3) Let a ∈ G be the canonical inclusion map Γ → T, i.e., χ 7→ χ(a).
   4) Then (X; ϕ) is isomorphic to (G, m; a).
In effect, we have proved the following result.

Theorem 17.11 (Halmos–von Neumann). Each ergodic measure-preserving sys-
tem with discrete spectrum is isomorphic to an ergodic rotation system on a compact
monothetic group.
More precisely, let (X; ϕ) be an ergodic measure-preserving system with discrete
spectrum. Then the set Γ of unimodular eigenvalues of the associated Koopman op-
erator is a subgroup of T, and (X; ϕ) is isomorphic to the rotation system (G, m; a),
where G = Γ ∗ is the dual group and a ∈ G is the canonical inclusion map Γ → T.

   This theorem is of considerable interest. We therefore give now a direct proof of
the Halmos–von Neumann theorem not relying on the Jacobs–de Leeuw–Glicksberg
theory. We follow the steps 1)–4) from the above.
Direct proof of Theorem 17.11. Let T be the Koopman operator of the ergodic sys-
tem (X; ϕ) with discrete spectrum, and let Γ := σp (T ) be its point spectrum. By
Proposition 7.18, each eigenvalue is unimodular and simple, and Γ is a subgroup of
T. Each eigenfunction is unimodular up to a multiplicative constant.
As a product of unimodular eigenfunctions is again an unimodular eigenfunction,

    Let us turn to some consequences of the Halmos–von Neumann theorem. The
first is another characterization of the Kronecker factor.
Corollary 17.12. Let (X; ϕ) be a measure-preserving system. Then Kro(X; ϕ) is the
largest factor of (X; ϕ) which is isomorphic to a compact group rotation system.
   The isomorphism problem consists in determining complete isomorphism in-
variants for (ergodic) measure-preserving systems, see for instance (Rédei and
Werndl 2012) for a historical account, but cf. also Section 18.4.7 below. The fol-
lowing corollary of the Halmos–von Neumann theorem states that for the class of


Published: Graduate Text in Mathematics, vol. 272, Springer-Verlag, 2015.
328                                    17 The Kronecker Factor and Systems with Discrete Spectrum

discrete spectrum systems the point spectrum of the Koopman operator is such a
complete isomorphism invariant.

Corollary 17.13. Two ergodic measure-preserving systems with discrete spectrum
are isomorphic if and only if the Koopman operators have the same point spectrum.

    Two measure-preserving systems (X; ϕ) and (Y; ψ) are called spectrally iso-
morphic if their Koopman operators on the L2 -spaces are unitarily equivalent, that
is, if there is a Hilbert space isomorphism (a unitary operator) S : L2 (X) → L2 (Y)
intertwining the Koopman operators, i.e., STϕ = Tψ S.

Corollary 17.14. Two ergodic measure-preserving systems with discrete spectrum
are (Markov) isomorphic if and only if they are spectrally isomorphic.

Proof. By Corollary 12.12 and by the remark following it, Markov isomorphic sys-
tems are spectrally isomorphic.
Conversely, if two ergodic measure-preserving systems are spectrally isomorphic,
their Koopman operators have the same point spectrum. Under the assumption that
both systems have discrete spectrum, they must be Markov isomorphic by Corollary
17.13.

Remark 17.15. The Halmos–von Neumann theorem dates back to the groundbreak-
ing article (Halmos and von Neumann 1942). There, continuous one-parameter
flows were considered and discrete spectrum systems were called systems with
“pure point spectrum”, cf. also Chapter 18. Mackey (1964) generalized that notion
to Borel actions on a standard probability space X of a locally compact separable
group Γ . In Mackey’s definition, such an action has “pure point spectrum” if L2 (X)
decomposes orthogonally into finite-dimensional irreducible subrepresentations of
Γ . His result is as follows.
Theorem (Mackey). Given any Borel action with pure point spectrum of a locally
compact separable group Γ on a standard probability space X, there is a compact
group G, a continuous homomorphism θ : Γ → G with dense image and a closed
subgroup H of G such that the action of Γ on X is isomorphic to the action of Γ on
the homogeneous space G/H by rotations via θ .
In our language, Mackey’s “pure point spectrum” just means that L2 (X) =
Kro(X; π(Γ )), where π : Γ → L (L2 (X)) is the associated representation. So
Mackey’s result is covered by Theorem 17.5. Of course, we employ the weaker no-
tion of Markov isomorphism instead of point isomorphism. However, this is backed
up by von Neumann’s Theorem 12.14 that allows to pass from Markov to point iso-
morphisms in case all involved probability spaces are standard. And this is the case
in Mackey’s situation: Since X is standard, L2 (X) is separable and consequently its
unitary group is Polish. A fortiori, the compact group G, being the strong closure of
π(Γ ), and finally its homogeneous space G/H are also Polish.




Published: Graduate Text in Mathematics, vol. 272, Springer-Verlag, 2015.
17.3 Disjointness of Weak Mixing and Discrete Spectrum                                329

17.3 Disjointness of Weak Mixing and Discrete Spectrum

Recall from Chapter 9 that a measure-preserving system (X; ϕ) is weakly mixing if
and only if it is ergodic and its Koopman operator has no eigenvalues except λ = 1
(Theorem 9.25). Since the Kronecker factor is generated by the eigenvectors, the
following is an equivalent reformulation.
Proposition 17.16. A measure-preserving system (X; ϕ) is weakly mixing if and
only if its Kronecker factor is trivial, i.e., Kro(X; ϕ) is isomorphic to a one-point
system.
   Proposition 17.16 states that the trivial system is the only one that is weakly
mixing and has discrete spectrum. Or, in Furstenberg’s terminology from (Fursten-
berg 1967), systems of discrete spectrum and weakly mixing systems are coprime:
A weakly mixing systems and a system with discrete spectrum spectrum can have
only the trivial system as a common factor.
   Proposition 17.16 can also be rephrased in terms of the notion of disjointness,
coined in (Furstenberg 1967) as well. According to Furstenberg, two systems are
disjoint if the product system is the only joining of the two systems. Since the con-
cept of a joining is not introduced in this book, we work here with an equivalent—
operator theoretic—definition, and refer to (Glasner 2003) for more details.
Definition 17.17. Two measure-preserving systems (X; ϕ) and (Y; ψ) are disjoint
if the projection S = 1 ⊗ 1 is the only Markov operator S ∈ M(Y; X) with Tϕ0 STψ = S.
   Note that we employ the identity Tϕ0 STψ = S instead of the stronger commuta-
tion relation STψ = Tϕ S. The reason is that we want disjointness to be a symmetric
property, and we do not require Tϕ to be invertible (in which case the two identities
are equivalent).
Proposition 17.18. A measure-preserving system (X; ϕ) is weakly mixing if and
only if it is disjoint from every system with discrete spectrum.
Proof. If (X; ϕ) is not weakly mixing, then its Kronecker factor is not trivial, and
hence the associated Markov embedding is not trivial.
Conversely, suppose that (Y; ψ) has discrete spectrum, (X; ϕ) is weakly mixing and
S ∈ M(Y; X) is a Markov operator satisfying S = Tϕ 0 STψ . Since Tϕ is a Markov
embedding, P := Tϕ Tϕ0 is a projection. Let 0 6= f ∈ L2 (Y) with Tψ f = λ f , |λ | = 1.
Then
                 Tϕ S f = Tϕ Tϕ0 STψ f = PSTψ f = PS(λ f ) = λ PS f .
Consequently, since Tϕ is isometric,

                             kS f k2 = Tϕ S f       2
                                                        = kPS f k2 ≤ kS f k2 .

As in the proof of Corollary 13.18 it follows that PS f = S f , and hence Tϕ S f = λ S f .
Since (X; ϕ) is weakly mixing, by Theorem 9.25 (or by Proposition 17.16) S f is a
constant function. Since (Y; ψ) has discrete spectrum, it follows that S maps L2 (Y)
to lin{1}, whence S = 1 ⊗ 1.


Published: Graduate Text in Mathematics, vol. 272, Springer-Verlag, 2015.
330                                    17 The Kronecker Factor and Systems with Discrete Spectrum

  We leave it as an exercise to show that, conversely, Proposition 17.16 is a conse-
quence of Proposition 17.18.
   Let us remark that we need not recur on the spectral characterization of weakly
mixing systems (Theorem 9.25) to obtain Proposition 17.16, because it is in fact a
consequence of the Jacobs–de Leeuw–Glicksberg theory developed in the previous
chapter. In order to see this, let

be the JdLG-decomposition of E := L2 (X) associated with the Koopman operator

compact groups yields that Erev is generated by the eigenvectors of T , cf. Theo-

subspace Eaws (T ) from Section 9.2. Since by Theorem 9.19(iv), the systems (X; ϕ)
is weakly mixing if and only if E = lin{1} ⊕ Eaws (T ), Proposition 17.16 follows
immediately.
But the Jacobs–de Leeuw–Glicksberg theory adds even more information since it
exploits the relative weak compactness of the semigroup {T n : n ≥ 0} on Lp (X),
p ∈ [1, ∞), a fact that played no role at all for the characterizations of weak mixing in
Chapter 9. Taking this weak compactness into account led to the characterizations of
the almost weakly stable part in Theorem 16.34. Applying that result to dynamical
systems (and summarizing the considerations from above) we obtain the following
theorem.

4. Skew Rotation

Consider the probability space X := (T2 , Bo(T2 ), m ⊗ m), where m is the Haar mea-
sure on T, and consider on X the skew rotation

                             ψa : T2 → T2 ,            ψ(z, w) := (az, zw),

see Example 5.15. The projection onto the first component is a point factor map

                                          (X; ψa ) → (T, m; a)

onto the rotation system (T, m; a). We claim: This factor coincides with the Kro-
necker factor.

Proof. Let T = Tψ and S be the Koopman operators of the skew rotation on T2
and the rotation system (T, m; a), respectively. The proof uses the same idea as the
proof of Proposition 10.17. Every function f ∈ L2 (T × T) can be written uniquely
as a series
                               f (z, w) = ∑ fn (z)wn
                                                      n∈Z

for certain fn    ∈ L2 (T). The equation T f = λ f then means that

                          ∑ λ fn (z)wn = λ f = T f = ∑ (S fn )(z)zn wn
                         n∈Z                                   n∈Z

which is equivalent to the infinite system of equations λ fn = zn S fn , n ∈ Z. We have
to show that fn = 0 whenever n 6= 0.
Now fix n 6= 0 and consider a function g ∈ L2 (T) with zn Sg = λ g. Writing as before
g = ∑ j∈Z a j z j , this translates into

                                     λ a j+n = a j a j        ( j ∈ Z).

Taking the modulus yields |a j+n | = |a j | for all j ∈ Z, but since ∑ j |a j |2 < ∞, it
follows that a j = 0 for all j ∈ Z. This concludes the proof.


5. Heisenberg Systems

Recall from Example 2.13 that the Heisenberg manifold is H := G/Γ , where G is
the non-Abelian group G of upper triangular real matrices with all diagonal entries
equal to one, i.e.,


Published: Graduate Text in Mathematics, vol. 272, Springer-Verlag, 2015.
336                                    17 The Kronecker Factor and Systems with Discrete Spectrum
                                     (                   )
                                       1xz
                                  G = 0 1 y : x, y, z ∈ R ,
                                       001
and Γ is its cocompact subgroup of elements with integer entries. Recall also the
notation                                       
                                            1xz
                             [x, y, z] := 0 1 y ,
                                            001
so that the multiplication takes the form

                           [a, b, c] · [x, y, z] = [a + x, b + y, c + z + ay].

We fix α = [a, b, c] ∈ G and consider the rotation system (H, m; α), where m is
the unique probability measure on H that is invariant under all (left) rotations by
elements of G, see Examples 5.16 and 5.17.
   This system has a rotation system on the two-dimensional torus R2 /Z2 ∼ = T2 as
a natural factor, given by the point factor map

                        H → R2 /Z2 ,             [x, y, z]Γ 7→ [x, y] (mod Z2 )

that intertwines multiplication with α and translation with [a, b] (mod Z2 ) . This
factor is called the rotation factor in the following. We claim: If a = b = 0, then
the Heisenberg system has discrete spectrum. Otherwise, the Kronecker factor is
precisely the rotation factor.

Proof. Note first (Exercise 5) that the center of G is
                                                      
           C := g ∈ G : gh = hg for all h ∈ G = [0, 0, r] : r ∈ R .

The compact Abelian group K := CΓ /Γ is isomorphic to R/Z. The restriction to
CΓ of the canonical left action of G on H induces a left action of K on H. Moreover,
the fixed factor associated with this action of K is precisely the rotation factor.
If a = b = 0, then α ∈ C and the translation by α embeds into the action of the
compact Abelian group K. Hence, by Corollary 15.18, the system (H, m; α) has
discrete spectrum. In the following we may therefore suppose that either a 6= 0 or
b 6= 0. We start with the case b 6= 0.
Denote, for g ∈ G, by Lg the Koopman operator on L2 (H) of the left rotation ξ Γ 7→
gξ Γ on H. Then Lgh = Lh Lg and Lg∗ = Lg−1 = Lg−1 , i.e., L : G → L2 (H) is a unitary
“anti-representation”. The Koopman operator of the system (H, m; α) is Lα , but
because of its special role we write T := Lα for it.
Let f ∈ L2 (H) and λ ∈ T such that T f = λ f . By the considerations above, it suffices
to show that Lh f = f for each h ∈ C. To this aim we shall employ a little “trick”,
whose operator theoretic content is deferred to Lemma 17.20 below. Its application
requires some preparatory computations.
Define, for x ∈ R, the element gx := [x, 0, 0] ∈ G and compute


Published: Graduate Text in Mathematics, vol. 272, Springer-Verlag, 2015.
17.4 Examples                                                                               337

                              α n gx α −n = [x, 0, nbx]          for n ∈ N0 ,
                                           r
see Exercise 6. For given r ∈ R let rn := bn (recall that b 6= 0). It follows that

                          grn → [0, 0, 0] and           α n grn α −n → [0, 0, r]          (17.1)

as n → ∞. Passing to Koopman operators, this translates into

                    Lgrn − T n∗ Lgrn T n → I − L[0,0,r]         strongly as n → ∞.

Now we employ Lemma 17.20 from below to conclude L[0,0,r] f = f . As r ∈ R was
arbitrary, it follows that f is contained in the fixed factor of the action of CΓ /Γ on
H, which is the rotation factor.
So the claim is proved in the case b 6= 0. If a 6= 0, one can employ a similar reasoning,
but with the vectors hx := [0, x, 0] replacing gx = [x, 0, 0].
Lemma 17.20. Let H be a Hilbert space, T ⊆ L (H) a semigroup of operators on
H and f ∈ H such that for each T ∈ T there is λT ∈ T with T f = λT f . Suppose
furthermore that R ∈ L (H) is a contraction with
                             
                f − R f ∈ clw S f − T ∗ ST f : T ∈ T , S ∈ L (H) .

Then f ∈ fix(R).
Proof. One has, for every T ∈ T and S ∈ L (H),

                  ( T ∗ ST f | f ) = ( ST f | T f ) = λT λT ( S f | f ) = ( S f | f ) .

It follows from the hypothesis that ( R f | f ) = ( f | f ). Since R is a contraction, this
implies that R f = f (Lemma D.14).
Remark 17.21. The central idea in the proof above is taken from (Einsiedler and
Ward 2011, p. 335). Lemma 17.20 is a generalization of the so-called (abstract)
Mautner phenomenon, see (Parry 1970, Sec. 1).
   As a result we obtain the following characterization.
Theorem 17.22. For a, b ∈ R the following assertions are equivalent:
   (i) The Heisenberg system (H, m; [a, b, c]) is ergodic.
  (ii) The topological Heisenberg system (H; [a, b, c]) is strictly ergodic.
 (iii) The numbers 1, a, b are rationally independent.
Proof. The equivalence of (i) and (iii) follows from the considerations above in
combination with Kronecker’s theorem (Theorem 14.18) and the fact that factors of
ergodic systems are ergodic. The implication (ii) ⇒ (i) is clear, since in this case m
is the unique and hence necessarily ergodic invariant probability measure on H. For
the remaining implication (i) ⇒ (ii) we employ Theorem 15.31 about compact group
extensions.


Published: Graduate Text in Mathematics, vol. 272, Springer-Verlag, 2015.
338                                    17 The Kronecker Factor and Systems with Discrete Spectrum

As seen above, the rotation factor is the fixed factor with respect to the action

              H × R/Z → H,                [x, y, z] · r := [x, y, z] · [0, 0, r] = [x, y, z + r]

by the compact group K = CΓ /Γ ∼  = R/Z. Hence, by Theorem 15.31 it suffices to
show that the measure m on H is the Haar lift’ of the Haar measure on the factor
R2 /Z2 with respect to the mean ergodic projection
                                                                     Z

where κ : R/Z → L (C(H)) is the associated Koopman representation. This is a
simple computation, left as Exercise 7.

The Spectral Theorem and Dynamical Systems




   By and large it is uniformly true that in mathematics there is a time lapse between a math-
   ematical discovery and the moment it becomes useful; and that this lapse can be anything
   from 30 to 100 years, in some cases even more; and that the whole system seems to func-
   tion without any direction, without any reference to usefulness, and without any desire to
   do things which are useful.
                                                                          John von Neumann

In this chapter we prove the spectral theorem for normal operators and study the cor-
responding spectral measures in some detail. In particular, we introduce the max-
imal spectral type and the multiplicity function yielding together a complete iso-
morphism invariant for unitary operators. Based on these fundamental results we
interpret various mixing properties in spectral terms and explain systems with dis-
crete spectrum from a point of view different from the one taken in Chapter 17.
In addition, a number of examples illuminates the fundamental ideas of the spectral
theory of dynamical systems. Readers interested in details and in the more advanced
theory can consult (Queffélec 1987), (Nadkarni 1998b), (Lemańczyk 1996), (Katok
and Thouvenot 2006), (Lemańczyk 2009), and the multitude of further references
therein.



18.1 The Spectral Theorem

A bounded operator T ∈ L (H) on a Hilbert space H is called normal if T ∗ T = T T ∗ ,
see Appendix D. For such an operator T its generated C∗ -algebra
                                       
                               A = alg I, T, T ∗

is commutative. Recall from Section 4.4 the definition of the Gelfand space Γ(A)
of A and denote by
                         
             SpA (T ) := λ ∈ C : λ I − T is not invertible within A


                                                                                             341
342                                                  18 The Spectral Theorem and Dynamical Systems

the spectrum of T as an element of the algebra A. We can also consider T as an
element of the full algebra L (H), and its spectrum there coincides with σ(T ), the
usual operator theoretic notion of spectrum. Then, trivially,

                                            σ(T ) ⊆ SpA (T ).

The next result shows that we have equality here.
Lemma 18.1. In the situation above SpA (T ) = σ(T ) and the evaluation map

                                   Γ(A) → σ(T ),             χ 7→ χ(T )

is a homeomorphism.
Proof. Let us abbreviate ρA (T ) := {λ ∈ ρ(T ) : (λ I − T )−1 ∈ A}. This set is closed
in ρ(T ). Indeed, let (λn )n∈N be a sequence in ρA (T ) with λn → λ ∈ ρ(A). Then,
since the resolvent mapping µ 7→ (µI − T )−1 is continuous, ((λn I − T )−1 )n∈N is
a Cauchy sequence in A, hence it is convergent to some limit in A which must be
(λ I − T )−1 .
Since ρA (T ) is also open and contains the set {λ ∈ C : |λ | > kT k}, it contains the
entire unbounded connected component of ρ(T ).
Now, fix λ ∈ ρ(T ). Then the operator S := (λ I − T )∗ (λ I − T ) is self-adjoint and
invertible. Since the spectrum of a self-adjoint operator is contained in R, the point
0 is an element of the unbounded component of ρ(S). By what we just have shown,
S−1 is an element of the C∗ -algebra generated by S, which is contained in A. Hence,
(λ I − T )−1 = S−1 (λ I − T )∗ ∈ A, and this implies that λ ∈ ρA (T ). It follows that
SpA (T ) = C \ ρA (T ) ⊆ C \ ρ(T ) = σ(T ).
For the remaining statement we note that the evaluation map is continuous (by the
definition of the topology on Γ(A)) and surjective (by Theorem 4.32). To see that it is
injective, note that any χ ∈ Γ(A) satisfies χ(T ∗ ) = χ(T ) by Lemma 4.35. In partic-
ular, χ is completely determined by its value on T . Since each bijective continuous
mapping between compact spaces is a homeomorphism, the proof is complete.
   By the lemma we may identify Γ(A) with σ (T ). From now on we abbreviate, for
simplicity,
                             K := σ (T ) ∼
                                         = Γ(A).

of C∗ -algebras. A moment’s thought reveals that Φ(T ) = (z 7→ z) is the coordinate

The Borel Functional Calculus

The functional calculus can be extended beyond continuous functions. Recall from
Appendix E.1 that BM(K) denotes the space of bounded Baire (=Borel) measurable
functions on K. If f ∈ BM(K) and x ∈ H, then f ∈ L2 (µx ) and hence f (T )x ∈ H has
been defined above as a compound expression, linear in f . By approximation (use,
e.g., Theorem 18.2.e),
                                               Z

                                               K

Hence, f (T ) is a linear operator (cf. Corollary D.6). The mapping

is called the (bounded) Borel functional calculus for T . (See Exercise 4 for an
alternative construction of the Borel functional calculus.) For the following result
recall the notion of a bp-convergent sequence from Appendix E.1.

Theorem 18.5 (Borel Functional Calculus). In the situation from above, the map-
ping Ψ : BM(K) → L (H) has the following properties:
    a) Ψ (z) = T .
   b) Ψ is a (contractive) homomorphism of C∗ -algebras.
    c) Ψ maps bp-convergent sequences to strongly convergent sequences.
   d) Every Ψ ( f ), f ∈ BM(K), commutes with every bounded operator on H that
      commutes with T and T ∗ .
Moreover, Ψ is uniquely determined by the properties a)–c).

Proof. a) is clear, and c) follows from the identity kΨ ( f )xk = k f (T )xk = k f kL2 (µx )
and from the fact that, by the dominated convergence theorem, bp-convergence im-
plies convergence in L2 (K, µx ).

for all x ∈ H. It follows that kΨ ( f )k ≤ k f k∞ .
Fix x ∈ H. Then f (T )g(T )x = ( f g)(T )x for all f , g ∈ C(K). By approximation this
identity remains valid for f ∈ C(K) and g ∈ L2 (µx ), in particular for g ∈ BM(K).
But then a second approximation argument establishes the identity for g ∈ BM(K)
and f ∈ L2 (µg(T )x ), and in particular for all f , g ∈ BM(K). In a similar way one can
show that Ψ ( f ) = Ψ ( f )∗ for all f ∈ BM(K). Thus, b) is proved.
To show d), suppose that S ∈ L (H) commutes with T and T ∗ . Then S f (T )x =
f (T )Sx for each x ∈ H and each f ∈ C(K). By approximation, this identity remains
valid for f ∈ L2 (µx ), in particular for f ∈ BM(K).
Finally, we prove uniqueness. Suppose that Ψ 0 : BM(K) → L (H) also has the
properties a)–c). Then E := { f ∈ BM(K) : Ψ ( f ) = Ψ 0 ( f )} is closed under bp-
convergence and contains the identity function z. Hence, it contains its conjugate
z and therefore all polynomials in z and z. But these are dense in C(K), by the
Stone–Weierstraß theorem, and hence C(K) ⊆ E. By Theorem E.1, it follows that
E = BM(K).

18.2 Spectral Decompositions and the Maximal Spectral Type

Before proceeding we need to recall some notions and facts from measure theory.
For simplicity, we restrict ourselves to measures on Ba(K) = Bo(K) for compact
subsets K of C.
   A measure ν ∈ M(K) is called absolutely continuous with respect to µ ∈ M(K),
in notation ν  µ, if

                   |µ| (B) = 0          =⇒     ν(B) = 0        for every B ∈ Bo(K).

The measures µ and ν are called mutually singular (denoted by µ ⊥ ν) if there
is B ∈ Bo(K) with |µ| (B) = 0 = |ν| (Bc ), and equivalent (µ ∼ ν) if µ  ν and
ν  µ. The basic properties of these relations are collected in Appendix B.10, in
particular in Lemma B.20.
Returning to spectral theory, we take T ∈ L (H) a normal operator on a Hilbert
space H, and (µx,y )x,y∈H the corresponding family of complex Borel (=Baire) mea-
sures on K := σ(T ).

Lemma 18.9. In this situation above the following assertions hold:
    a) One has µ f (T )x = | f |2 µx for all x ∈ H and f ∈ L2 (µx ). In particular, if x ∈ H
       and y ∈ Z(x), then µy  µx . Conversely, if x ∈ H and µ ∈ M+ (K) is such
       that µ  µx , then there is y ∈ Z(x) with µ = µy .
   b) For x, y ∈ H,

                              µx ⊥ µy    =⇒        µx,y = 0         ⇐⇒       Z(x) ⊥ Z(y);

         and if x, y ∈ Z(u) for some u ∈ H, then µx ⊥ µy ⇔ Z(x) ⊥ Z(y).
    c) µx ∼ µy if and only if the operators T |Z(x) and T |Z(y) are unitarily equivalent.

Theorem 18.10. For I, J ⊆ M(K) closed ideals the following assertions hold:
    a) H(I) is a closed T -bi-invariant subspace of H.
   b) If I ∩ J = {0}, then I ⊕ J is a closed ideal and

                                           H(I ⊕ J) = H(I) ⊕ H(J)

         is an orthogonal decomposition.
Proof. a) This follows from (18.6). Note that µT x,y = µx,T ∗ y and µT ∗ x,y = µx,Ty for
all x, y ∈ H.
b) By (18.5) and Lemma B.20, kµ + νk = |µ + ν| (K) = |µ| (K) + |ν| (K) = kµk +
kνk for µ ∈ I and ν ∈ J. Hence, the canonical projection

                                   PI : I + J → I,          µ + ν 7→ µ

is bounded. Since I and J are closed, they are complete; therefore, I + J is complete,
hence closed.
To see that I +J is an ideal, suppose that µ ∈ I, ν ∈ J and ρ ∈ M(K) with ρ  µ +ν.
Then there are µ 0 , ν 0 ∈ M(K) with µ 0  µ and ν 0  ν and ρ = µ 0 + ν 0 ∈ I + J
(Exercise 10).
In order to prove orthogonality, let x ∈ H(I) and y ∈ H(J). Then, by (18.6), µx,y ∈ I
and µx,y = µy,x ∈ J since an ideal is conjugation-invariant. By hypothesis, µx,y = 0,
which implies that x ⊥ y, by Lemma 18.9.c).
Finally, we show that H(I ⊕ J) = H(I) ⊕ H(J). Only the inclusion “⊆” needs to be
shown. Let u ∈ H(I + J), i.e., µu = µ + ν for some measures µ ∈ I and ν ∈ I. Since
µu ≥ 0, taking the modulus yields µu = |µ + ν| = |µ| + |ν| and hence µ = |µ| ≥ 0
and ν = |ν| ≥ 0.
Now, since µu = µ + ν, both µ and ν are absolutely continuous with respect to µu .
By Lemma 18.9 there are x, y ∈ Z(u) with µx = µ and µy = ν. Take f , g ∈ L2 (µu )

with x = f (T )u and y = g(T )u. Then µx = | f |2 µx and µy = |g|2 µu , and hence

               µu = µ + ν = µx + µy = | f |2 µu + |g|2 µu = (| f |2 + |g|2 )µu .

Remarks 18.14. 1) Theorem 18.12 about the maximal spectral type µmax is just
a part of a more sophisticated result. Indeed, one can find a (possibly finite) sequence
(xn )n∈N with
                            µx1  µx2  · · ·  µxn  · · ·
and such that
                                                    ∞

is an orthogonal decomposition. Each measure µxn is uniquely determined up to
equivalence, and [µx1 ] = [µmax ] is the maximal spectral type.


Published: Graduate Text in Mathematics, vol. 272, Springer-Verlag, 2015.
354                                                  18 The Spectral Theorem and Dynamical Systems

   Even more is true: There is a decreasing sequence (Bn )n∈N of Borel sets and a
sequence (yn )n∈N of vectors of H such that

                   Z(xn ) = Z(yn ), i.e., µxn ∼ µyn           and     µyn = 1Bn µmax .

This leads to the definition of the multiplicity function,

                               M : K → N0 ∪ {∞},             M := ∑ 1Bn ,
                                                                     n∈N

and to a more precise description of properties of T . The maximal spectral type and
the multiplicity function together provide a complete set of invariants for unitary
equivalence of normal operators. Therefore, they play a central role in the spectral
analysis of dynamical systems. Below, in Section 18.4 we shall present some basic
results of that theory. The previous decomposition and the corresponding results
are sometimes referred to as the Hahn–Hellinger theorem. For more details see
(Nadkarni 1998b, Ch. 1).
   2) A normal operator T ∈ L (H) is said to have simple spectrum if for the
multiplicity function M = 1 almost everywhere with respect to µmax . Two operators
with simple spectrum are unitarily equivalent if and only if their maximal spectral
types are equal. For a characterization of simple spectrum we refer to Exercise 9.
   3) The separability assumption about H cannot be easily dispensed with as the
following example shows. Consider H = `2 (T) and the unitary operator T ∈ L (H)
defined by T f (z) := z f (z). It is easy to see that each Dirac measure δλ , λ ∈ T, arises
as µ f for some f ∈ H.
   On the other hand, no µ ∈ M(T) can have the property that δλ  µ for each
λ ∈ T. Hence, our definition of maximal spectral type is of no use here. (There are,
however, definitions of the spectral type and the multiplicity function that work for
the nonseparable case, see (Halmos 1998) and (Brown 1974).)

   By the definition of the maximal spectral type, we have H(µmax ) = H. Hence,
according to Corollary 18.11, any mutually singular decomposition of µmax provides
an orthogonal decomposition of the space H into T -bi-invariant closed subspaces.
We shall look at a particular example in the following section.



18.3 Discrete Measures and Eigenvalues

In this section we study eigenvalues and eigenvectors through the spectral theo-

below).

Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors

As always in this chapter, let T be a bounded normal operator on a Hilbert space H
with associated family (µx,y )x,y∈H of complex measures on K = σ(T ). The following
result characterizes eigenvalues and eigenspaces of T via the functional calculus.
Proposition 18.15. In the situation just described let x ∈ H and λ ∈ C.
    a) The following assertions are equivalent:
            (i) T x = λ x.
            (ii)   f (T )x = f (λ )x for all f ∈ BM(K).
           (iii) µx,y = ( x | y ) δλ for all y ∈ H.
           (iv) µx = kxk2 δλ .

Discrete and Continuous Measures

Recall from Appendix B.10 that a complex Borel measure µ on K is called contin-
uous if µ{a} = 0 for every a ∈ K, and discrete if there are sequences (λn )n∈N in C
and (an )n∈N in K such that
                                 µ = ∑ λn δan .
                                                   n∈N

By Proposition B.27, the sets Mc (K) and Md (K) of, respectively, continuous and
discrete measures on K are closed ideals of M(K) satisfying

                                     M(K) = Md (K) ⊕ Mc (K).                               (18.8)

and                       Hc := x ∈ H : µx is continuous .

Proposition 18.17. For a normal operator T ∈ L (H) we have
                           
                   Hd = lin x ∈ H : x is an eigenvector of T .

Proof. If x ∈ H is an eigenvector of T with eigenvalue λ ∈ C, then µx = kxk2 δλ , and
hence x ∈ Hd . Conversely, suppose that x ∈ Hd , i.e., µx is discrete. Then µx (Ac ) = 0
for a countable set A ⊆ K. By (18.4) and by Theorem 18.5.c) it follows that x =
PA x = ∑λ ∈A Pλ x. Since Pλ x ∈ ker(λ I − T ), the proof is complete.

Wiener’s Lemma

Let µ ∈ M(T) be a positive measure, let H := L2 (T, µ)m and let the operator T ∈

C(T). Hence, for f , g ∈ H and h ∈ C(T)

                                               µ f ,g = f gµ.

18.4 Dynamical Systems

We now apply the previously developed theory to measure-preserving systems
(X; ϕ). In order to employ the spectral theorem, we shall consider only invertible
systems here. This is, however, not a strong restriction, as we can always pass to the
invertible extension, see Section 13.5. (Passing to the invertible extension of a sys-
tem (X; ϕ) is essentially equivalent with passing to the minimal unitary dilation of
its Koopman operator, compare the construction on page 252 with Example D.30.)
    For statements that involve the maximal spectral type, it will be convenient to
suppose further that the occurring probability space X is such that the space L2 (X)
is separable. This is the case if and only if (X; ϕ) is—up to isomorphism—a standard
system (Definition 6.8).


1. Systems with Discrete Spectrum

Recall that a measure-preserving system (X; ϕ) is said to have discrete spectrum if
its Koopman operator T on L2 (X) has discrete spectrum, which by definition means
that L2 (X) is generated by the eigenvectors of T . We can now make sense of this
terminology.
Corollary 18.22. A unitary operator T on a Hilbert space H has discrete spectrum
if and only if each µx , x ∈ H, is a discrete measure. In particular, if H is separable,
then T has discrete spectrum if and only if µmax is a discrete measure.
Proof. Since all eigenvalues of a unitary operator are unimodular, T has discrete
spectrum if and only if H = Hd (cf. Proposition 18.17).
    Discrete measures are possibly infinite sums of point measures. Therefore, in-
stead of “discrete spectrum” also the term pure point spectrum is used, especially
in the older literature.


2. Mixing Properties

Let (X; ϕ) be an invertible measure-preserving system with Koopman operator T on
L2 (X). Since T leaves the constant functions fixed, it is only interesting what hap-
pens on the orthogonal complement 1⊥ . Therefore, spectral properties of a measure-
preserving system are usually defined in terms of the restriction T0 of T to 1⊥ . If
L2 (X) is separable, we may speak of its maximal spectral type, denoted by [µ0 ] and
called the (restricted) maximal spectral type of the measure-preserving system.
Corollary 18.23. An invertible standard system (X; ϕ) is ergodic if and only if its
maximal spectral type [µ0 ] satisfies µ0 {1} = 0.
Proof. By Proposition 18.15 µ0 {1} = 0 if and only if dim fix(T0 ) = 0, which holds
if and only if dim fix(T ) = 1 being equivalent to ergodicity by Proposition 7.15.


Published: Graduate Text in Mathematics, vol. 272, Springer-Verlag, 2015.
360                                                  18 The Spectral Theorem and Dynamical Systems

   Next, let us turn to weakly mixing systems.

Proposition 18.24. Let T be a unitary operator on a separable Hilbert space H with
maximal spectral type [µmax ]. Then T is almost weakly stable if and only if µmax is
a continuous measure.

Proof. This follows from Corollary 18.18. Alternatively, avoiding the JdLG-theory,
one can argue as follows:
By definition, µ̂x,y (−n) = ( T n x | y ) for all x, y ∈ H and n ∈ N. Since µmax is con-
tinuous if and only if µx,y is continuous for every x, y ∈ H, the claim follows from
Wiener’s lemma (Proposition 18.20), cf. also Remark 18.21.

   Proposition 18.24 together with Theorem 9.19 leads to the following result.

Corollary 18.25 (Weak Mixing). An invertible standard system (X; ϕ) is weakly
mixing if and only if µ0 is a continuous measure.

    In order to describe strong mixing in spectral terms we need the following no-
tion. A Borel measure µ ∈ M(T) is called a Rajchman measure if its Fourier coef-
ficients µ̂(n) converge to 0 for |n| → ∞. The Haar measure m on T (and any measure
being absolutely continuous with respect to m) is a Rajchman measure, this is the
Riemann–Lebesgue lemma. We refer to (Lyons 1995) for a survey on Rajchman
measures.

Lemma 18.26. The set of Rajchman measures
                        
             MR (T) := µ ∈ M(T) : µ is a Rajchman measure

is a closed ideal of M(T).

Proof. It is straightforward to prove that MR (T) is a closed subspace of M(T). Fix
µ ∈ MR (T) and h ∈ BM(T) with |h| = 1 and µ = h |µ|. Since the mapping

                            L1 (|µ|) → M(K),               f 7→ f µ = f h |µ|

is isometric, the space
                                   
                               F := f ∈ L1 (|µ|) : f µ ∈ MR (T)

is a closed subspace of L1 (|µ|). Since for k ∈ Z

                                  d
                                  zk µ(n) = µ̂(n − k)             (n ∈ Z)

and µ ∈ MR (T), F contains the trigonometric polynomials, hence C(T), and hence
is equal to all of L1 (|µ|). It follows that L1 (|µ|) ⊆ MR (T).

   From Lemma 18.26 we obtain a spectral characterization of the weak stability of
a normal contraction.

   Proposition 18.27 together with Theorem 9.6 leads to the following result.

Corollary 18.28 (Strong Mixing). An invertible standard system (X; ϕ) is strongly
mixing if and only if its maximal spectral type [µ0 ] consists of Rajchman measures.

   A unitary operator T on a separable Hilbert space H is said to have Lebesgue
spectrum if its maximal spectral type is [µmax ] = [m], where m is the Haar measure
on T (the normalized Lebesgue measure). An invertible standard system is said to
have Lebesgue spectrum if the restriction T0 of its Koopman operator T to 1⊥ has
Lebesgue spectrum.

Proposition 18.29. An invertible standard system with Lebesgue spectrum is
strongly mixing.

Proof. Consider a Bernoulli shift B(p0 , . . . , pk−1 ) = (X; τ), i.e., X = (Wk , Σ , µ) with

Moreover, as easily seen, dim H0 = ∞, hence by Proposition 18.32 the system has

   Corolary 18.33 implies that different Bernoulli shifts cannot be distinguished
by purely spectral information. It had been an open problem for quite some time
whether (nontrivial, invertible) Bernoulli shifts are all isomorphic. Only when Kol-
mogorov (1958) introduced the fundamental concept of entropy, could this prob-
lem be solved in the negative. (Komogorov’s definition was later adjusted by Sinaı̆
(1959), whence the now common name Kolmogorov–Sinaı̆ entropy.)
   We shall not give the definition of entropy here, but contend ourselves with stat-
ing that it is an isomorphism invariant and that the entropy of the Bernoulli shift
B(p0 , . . . , pk−1 ) (invertible or noninvertible) can be computed as
                                                           k−1
                               H(p0 , . . . , pk−1 ) = − ∑ p j log2 (p j )
                                                            j=0

(with the convention 0 · log2 (0) := 0). Isomorphic Bernoulli shifts must possess the
same entropy and, by a famous theorem of Ornstein (1970a), the converse is also
true.
Theorem 18.34 (Ornstein). Two two-sided Bernoulli shifts over standard proba-
bility state spaces are isomorphic if and only if they have the same entropy.
For instance, the two-sided Bernoulli shifts B( 21 , 81 , 18 , 18 , 18 ) and B( 14 , 14 , 14 , 14 ) are iso-
morphic, while B( 21 , 21 ) and B( 41 , 14 , 14 , 14 ) are not.
    The previous theorem applies also to two-sided shifts with infinite entropy
(this is only possible if the state space is infinite), see (Ornstein 1970b). How-
ever, it fails for the class of all Bernoulli shifts, as a one-sided and a two-
sided Bernoulli shift with the same probability vector (p0 , . . . , pk−1 ) are not iso-
morphic but have the same entropy. Moreover, and not that obviously, it also
fails for the class of one-sided Bernoulli shifts since, for example, the one-sided


Published: Graduate Text in Mathematics, vol. 272, Springer-Verlag, 2015.
364                                                  18 The Spectral Theorem and Dynamical Systems

shifts B( 12 , 81 , 81 , 81 , 18 ) and B( 14 , 14 , 41 , 14 ) are not isomorphic. In fact, two one-sided
Bernoulli shifts B(p0 , . . . , pk−1 ) and B(q0 , . . . , qm−1 ) are isomorphic if and only if
k = m and the probability vectors (p0 , . . . , pk−1 ) and (q0 , . . . , qm−1 ) are permutations
of each other, see (Walters 1973).
Finally, we remark that entropy is not a complete isomorphism invariant for invert-
ible ergodic standard systems: Each ergodic group rotation (G, m; a) with G being a
metrizable compact group, has zero entropy (see, e.g., (Walters 1982, Thm. 4.25)).
   We recommend Walters’ standard book (1982) for a quick introduction to the
theory of entropy, and (Katok 2007) for a survey on the history as well as the most
recent developments. The articles (Palm 1976b) and (Palm 1976a) contain an ab-
stract, lattice theoretic approach to entropy. For more results on entropy one can
consult the books (Billingsley 1965), (Parry 1969a), (Ornstein 1974), (Sinaı̆ 1976),
(England and Martin 1981), (Cornfeld et al. 1982), (Petersen 1989), (Downarow-
icz 2011).


4. Kolmogorov Automorphisms

Let (X; ϕ) be an invertible standard system, X = (X, Σ , µ). The mapping ϕ is called
a Kolmogorov automorphism (K-automorphism for short) if there is a sub-σ -
algebra Σ 0 of Σ with the following properties:
   (i) Σ 0 ⊆ ϕΣ 0 ,
                                            ∞

                                              n=0

where the equality of sets is understood in the measure algebra, i.e., almost every-
where. The system (X; ϕ) is then called a K-system.
It is Exercise 23 to show that a two-sided Bernoulli shift is a K-system (see also,
e.g., (Walters 1982, Thm. 4.30)). By a result of Ornstein (1971) not every K-system
is isomorphic to a Bernoulli shift. This implies that entropy alone is not a complete
isomorphism invariant for the class of K-systems. This becomes particularly inter-
esting in view of the next result (for a proof we refer to (Rokhlin 1967, §14) or
(Walters 1982, Thm. 4.33)).
Theorem 18.35 (Rokhlin). Each nontrivial K-system (X; ϕ) has countable
Lebesgue spectrum, and in particular, is strongly mixing and spectrally isomorphic
to each nontrivial two-sided Bernoulli shift.
