6. Automorphisms on Groups

Let G be a compact metric Abelian group, and let ϕ : G → G be a continuous1 group
automorphism. The Haar measure m is invariant with respect to ϕ (Exercise 24),
thus (G, m; ϕ) is a measure-preserving system. Our aim is to prove that if (G, m; ϕ)
is ergodic, then (G, m; ϕ) has countable Lebesgue spectrum and, hence, that it is
strongly mixing.
   Obviously, the Koopman operator T := Tϕ on L2 (G, m) of ϕ maps characters to
characters, and restricts to an automorphism of the dual group G∗ .
Proposition 18.37 (Halmos, Rokhlin). The measure-preserving system (G, m; ϕ)
is ergodic if and only if the group automorphism T := Tϕ : G∗ → G∗ has no pe-
riodic points other than the trivial character 1. As a consequence, every ergodic
automorphism (G, m; ϕ) is totally ergodic.
Proof. Suppose that the system (G, m; ϕ) is ergodic. Let χ ∈ G∗ be such that T n χ =
χ for some n ∈ N being minimal with this property. Then we have (T j χ |χ ) = 0 for
j = 1, . . . , n − 1 by minimality of n since different characters are orthogonal. For

                                     f := χ + T χ + · · · + T n−1 χ,

we have T f = f and hence, by ergodicity, f = c1. This implies, provided χ 6= 1,

                        c = ( f | 1) = 0       and      |c|2 = ( f | f ) = n > 0,

which is impossible.
For the proof of the converse implication let f ∈ L2 (G, m) be with T f = f . By
looking at its Fourier expansion we obtain for each n ∈ N

                                ∑ ∗ aχ T n χ = T n f = f = ∑ ∗ aχ χ.
                               χ∈G                                χ∈G


If the characters χ, T ±1 χ, . . . , T ±n χ, . . . are all different, then we conclude aT n χ =
aχ for each n ∈ Z. In this case we must have aχ = 0. Therefore, if aχ 6= 0, then there
is n ∈ N with T n χ = χ. But then χ = 1 by assumption, i.e., f is constant.
The last assertion follows from the fact that Tϕ has nontrivial periodic points if and
only if Tϕ k does (for some/all k ∈ N).
1 A Borel measurable automorphism ϕ : G → G is automatically continuous, see Exercise 15.16,

or (Banach 1932, Ch. 1, Thm. 4), (Hewitt and Ross 1979, Thm. 22.18).


Published: Graduate Text in Mathematics, vol. 272, Springer-Verlag, 2015.
18.4 Dynamical Systems                                                                367

   The following result was found independently by Halmos and Rokhlin. For a
proof, which is purely group theoretic, we refer to (Halmos 1956, p. 54).
Lemma 18.38. Let A be a nontrivial Abelian group and let ϕ be an automorphism
of A. Suppose that the orbits of ϕ different from {1} are all infinite. Then ϕ has
infinitely many orbits.
   We can now prove the result promised at the beginning.
Theorem 18.39. Let G be a nontrivial compact metrizable Abelian group and let
ϕ : G → G be a continuous automorphism of G. If (G, m; ϕ) is ergodic, then it has
countable Lebesgue spectrum. In particular, it is strongly mixing.
Proof. Let χ ∈ G∗ be a nontrivial character. Then T n χ 6= χ by Proposition 18.37 and
hence ( T n χ | χ ) = 0 for every n ∈ N. This yields that (T n χ)n∈Z is an orthonormal
basis in the cyclic subspace Z(χ). Since the Koopman operator T is an automor-
phism of the dual group G∗ , and the orbits are all infinite by Proposition 18.37,
Lemma 18.38 yields that T has infinitely many orbits, and by assumption actually
countably many. Therefore, we can take a sequence (χk )k∈N in G∗ such that
                                              [
                                      G∗ =          T n χk : n ∈ Z
                                              k∈N

with the sets on the right-hand side being disjoint. We therefore obtain
                                                        M
                                        L2 (G, m) =           Z(χk ),
                                                        k∈N

and an application of Proposition 18.32 concludes the proof.
   As a consequence, if ϕ is an ergodic automorphism of the d-dimensional torus
Td , then the measure-preserving system (Td , m; ϕ) is spectrally isomorphic to a
Bernoulli shift. In (1971) Katznelson proved that such systems are (point) isomor-
phic to Bernoulli shifts.
   After several other particular cases had been established, Lind (1977) and, inde-
pendently Miles and Thomas (1978a), (1978b) found the following beautiful result.
Theorem 18.40 (Lind–Miles–Thomas). Let G be a compact metrizable Abelian
group and let ϕ : G → G be a continuous automorphism of G. If the system (G, m; ϕ)
is ergodic, then it is (point) isomorphic to a Bernoulli shift.


7. The Isomorphism Problem

The first explicit formulation of the isomorphism problem goes back to von Neu-
mann (1932c), where he wrote on page 593:
   Daß die Koopmansche Methode wirklich alle Wahrscheinlichkeitsfragen der klassischen
   Mechanik erfaßt, wäre belegt, wenn wir wüßten, daß alle isomorphieinvarianten Eigen-
   schaften auch unitär invariant sind.


Published: Graduate Text in Mathematics, vol. 272, Springer-Verlag, 2015.
368                                                  18 The Spectral Theorem and Dynamical Systems

In free translation and in our terminology this reads as:
   That the method of Koopman indeed answers all probabilistic questions of classical me-
   chanics would be established if we knew that all (point) isomorphism invariants are also
   invariants for spectral isomorphism.

Yet in other words: Is it true that spectrally isomorphic systems are isomorphic?
A few years later this question was answered in the negative by Halmos and von
Neumann himself, as sketched in §11 of the survey article by Halmos (1949). But
no detailed paper of them was published on this matter, and their solution became
obscured. Rédei and Werndl have traced back the sources and found a letter of
von Neumann to Ulam from 1941 describing the same counterexample. We re-
fer to (Rédei and Werndl 2012) where the full story is told and where also von
Neumann’s letter can be found along with some historical information on the iso-
morphism problem and its later developments. The example of von Neumann and
Halmos is in Exercise 26. In what follows, we present the solution of Anzai (1951)
that can be based on arguments similar to the ones for the skew rotation above.
For given m ∈ N consider the measure-preserving system (T2 , mT2 ; ψa,m ) given by

                                        ψa,m (x, y) = (ax, xm y),

where a ∈ T is not a root of unity. Recall from Exercise 17.9 that this system is
strictly ergodic and its Kronecker factor is the rotation factor (T, m; a)
                                       
                             Kro = lin e j ⊗ 1 : j ∈ Z .

Now, by analogous calculations as in Section 18.4.5 above, one can establish the
following.
Proposition 18.41.    a) The Koopman operator T := Tψa,m (on E = L2 (T2 )) of
                    2
      the system (T , mT2 ; ψa,m ) has countable Lebesgue spectrum when restricted
      to the almost weakly stable part Eaws .
   b) These systems are spectrally isomorphic for all m ∈ N.
The proof is left as Exercise 25. Combining this with the next result yields noniso-
morphic but spectrally isomorphic systems.

    a) The point isomorphisms between the systems (T2 , mT2 ; ψa,m ) and

                     θ2 (ax, xm y) = bk xk θ2 (x, y) for almost all x, y ∈ T.       (18.11)

Chapter 19
Topological Dynamics and Colorings




   La couleur est mon obsession quotidienne, ma joie et mon tourment.1
                                                                           Claude Monet2

In this chapter we show the connection between coloring results from combinatorics
and topological dynamical systems, an aspect that was discovered by Furstenberg
and Weiss. Since their seminal paper (Furstenberg and Weiss 1978b) a new area has
emerged where even today active research goes on.
A basic result is the classical theorem of van der Waerden (1927) about arithmetic
progressions. An arithmetic progression of length k ∈ N is a set A of natural num-
bers of the form
                                                      
          A := a, a + n, a + 2n, . . . , a + (k − 1)n = a + jn : 0 ≤ j < k

for some a, n ∈ N. The number a is called the starting point and n the difference
of this arithmetic progression. An arithmetic progression of length k is also called
a k-term arithmetic progression. A subset A ⊆ N is called AP-rich if it contains
arbitrarily long (finite) arithmetic progressions, or which is the same, it contains
k-term arithmetic progressions for every k ∈ N.
Theorem 19.1 (Van der Waerden). If one colors the natural numbers with finitely
many colors, then there is a monochromatic AP-rich set. In other words: If N =
A1 ∪ A2 ∪ . . . ∪ Ar for some r ∈ N, then there exists j0 ∈ {1, . . . , r} such that for every
k ∈ N there are a, n ∈ N such that

                         a, a + n, a + 2n, . . . , a + (k − 1)n ∈ A j0 .

One aspect of combinatorial number theory deals with similar questions: If we color
the natural numbers with finitely many colors arbitrarily, is there a monochromatic
part in which a specific structure can be found?
1 Color is my day-long obsession, joy and torment.
2 Encyclopédie Larousse: Claude Monet




                                                                                          375
376                                                             19 Topological Dynamics and Colorings

We shall actually prove van der Waerden’s theorem in two ways, and in strengthened
versions at that. As a preparation we investigate the Stone–Čech compactification
βS of a discrete semigroup S, and on our way we shall encounter Hindman’s the-
orem about colorings of N. We first prove van der Waerden’s theorem by utilizing
the right-topological semigroup βN and deduce then a generalization of Birkhoff’s
recurrence theorem from it. But that is not the whole story: We prove this latter gen-
eralization, the Furstenberg–Weiss multiple recurrence theorem, by a direct and el-
ementary topological argument, and deduce from it combinatorial statements, such
as the Gallai–Witt theorem. Thus closing the circle, we present an introduction to
the fascinating interplay between topological dynamics and combinatorial number
theory.



19.1 The Stone–Čech Compactification

First we take a small detour to explore the C∗ -algebra
                          
                 `∞ (S) := x : x is a bounded function from S to C

in some detail, where S is a nonempty set. On S we shall consider the discrete
topology. The operations are defined pointwise, and the norm is given by

                                           kxk∞ = sup |x(s)| .
                                                      s∈S

Denote by βS the Gelfand representation space of `∞ (S), and recall from Section 4.4
that βS is the space the set of nonzero multiplicative linear functionals on `∞ (S). The
space βS carries the weak∗ topology of (`∞ (S))0 restricted to βS, and by Gelfand’s
theory one has the isomorphism

                               `∞ (S) ≃ C(βS),          x 7→ (p 7→ p(x)).

In βS there are the point-evaluations δs for all s ∈ S. If we identify s with δs , we can
consider S as a subset of βS. Notice also that by Theorem 7.23 every p ∈ βS is a
positive functional.
Proposition 19.2. The mapping

                                      ι : S → βS,       s 7→ δs ∈ βS

is a homeomorphism onto its image, when S is endowed with the discrete topology.
Furthermore, the image ι(S) is dense.
Proof. The mapping ι is trivially injective, and it is continuous since S is discrete.
Let s0 ∈ S and ε > 0 be given. For s ∈ S define x(s) := ε if s 6= s0 and set x(s0 ) = 0.
Then x ∈ `∞ (S), and |x(s) − x(s0 )| < ε holds if and only if s = s0 , i.e., when δs = δs0 .
This proves that ι is a homeomorphism.

previous proposition we may identify S with a dense subspace of βS when conve-

Proposition 19.3. Let x : S → C be a bounded (continuous) function. Then there is
a unique continuous extension xe : βS → C.

                                                   xe(p) := p(x).
Continuity of xe follows since βS has the restriction of the weak∗ topology
σ (`∞ (S)0 , `∞ (S)).

s ∈ S. By Urysohn’s Lemma 4.2 we have x(s) = xe(s), i.e., xe is an extension of x.

It can be easily seen that up to homeomorphism βS is the unique compact topolog-

βS is called the Stone–Čech compactification of the discrete space S.

                                            lim x(s) := xe(p),

where xe is furnished by the proposition above. We call lims→p x(s) the p-limit of x.

                                    

The terminology “p-limit” is underlined by the proposition below showing that non-
trivial elements of βN extend the usual notion of the limit of convergent sequences.
We first need a lemma.

Lemma 19.6.            a) Let p ∈ βS and A ⊆ S. Then p(1A ) ∈ {0, 1}.
   b) If p ∈ βS \ S, then p(1A ) = 0 for every finite set A ⊆ S.
    c) If S = A1 ∪ A2 ∪ · · · ∪ Ar , then there is j0 ∈ {1, . . . , r} with p(1 j0 ) = 1.

                           p(1A )2 = p(1A )p(1A ) = p(1A 1A ) = p(1A ),

which implies the assertion.
b) Let p ∈ βS \ S, and notice first that p is also a positive functional (see Theorem

this is not so, by part a) we have p(1{a} ) = 1, and by additivity p(1S\{a} ) = 0. For a
positive function x ∈ `∞ (S) we have

          x(a) = p(x(a)1{a} ) ≤ p(x) ≤ p(x(a)1{a} ) + kxk∞ p(1S\{a} ) = x(a).

This shows that p = δa , contradicting the choice of p.
c) Since p is a positive functional, 1 = p(1) ≤ p(1A1 ) + p(1A2 ) + · · · + p(1Ar ). By
part a) p(1A j ) ∈ {0, 1}, hence the assertion follows.

19.2 The Semigroup Structure of βS

We now suppose that S is a semigroup and extend the semigroup structure from S to
βS. Denote by Lr the left rotation on `∞ (S) by an element r ∈ S, i.e.,
                                       
                                   Lr x (s) = x(rs).

(In case of S = N we speak of translation (Lm x)(n) = x(m + n).) Now, given an
element p ∈ βS and a function x ∈ `∞ (S), the function

                                            r 7→ p(Lr x) ∈ C

is bounded. So for two elements p, q ∈ βS we can define their convolution by
                                                            
                 (p ∗ q)(x) := p r 7→ q(Lr x) = lim lim x(rs) .
                                                                  r→p s→q

The next proposition summarizes the algebraic properties of this operation.
Proposition 19.8.           a) For s, t ∈ S we have

                                            (p ∗ q) ∗ u = p ∗ (q ∗ u),

         i.e., ∗ is associative, hence (βS, ∗) is a semigroup.

              δs ∗ δt (x) = δs (r 7→ δt (Lr x)) = δs (r 7→ x(rt)) = x(st) = δst (x).

Since the mapping s 7→ δs is injective, we may identify s with δs . So by virtue of a)
we can consider S as a subsemigroup of βS.
The next proposition describes continuity properties of the convolution. Recall again
that the topology on βS is the weak∗ topology of `∞ (S)0 restricted to βS, and that we

Proposition 19.9.           a) For each p ∈ βS the right multiplication by p

         is continuous on βS.
   b) For each s ∈ S the left multiplication by s

         is continuous on βS.

if q0 is such that |(q − q0 )(y)| < ε for y(r) := p(Lr x).

   Exercise 2 shows that the left multiplication by an arbitrary element is not always
continuous, in particular βS is not commutative in general. Especially this applies
to βN. Nevertheless, from now on we shall use the symbol + for the operation ∗
in βN and in βS when S is commutative. Furthermore, we note that even if S is
a group the resulting compactification βS need not be so. In fact, it may contain
                                                                                    ℵ
many idempotents, hence in general is not a group. For example βN contains 22 0
idempotents, see (Hindman and Strauss 1998, Ch. 6).

Proof. The statement for scalar-valued sequences is just the definition of the convo-

19.3 Topological Dynamics Revisited

We now return to topological dynamical systems where the semigroup βN will yield
new insights. In what follows, we shall write p + q instead of p ∗ q even though this
operation is noncommutative.
Proposition 19.11. Let (K; ϕ) be a topological system. For x ∈ K and p ∈ βN we
define
                              ϕ p (x) := lim ϕ n (x).
                                                      n→p

Then                                         
                                         E := ϕ p : p ∈ βN
is a semigroup of transformations on K. The mapping Φ : βN 3 p 7→ ϕ p ∈ E is a
semigroup homomorphism, continuous if E is endowed with the topology of point-
wise convergence.

Proof. For p, q ∈ βN we have by Propositions 19.10 and 19.5 that
                                                                     
       ϕ p+q (x) = lim lim ϕ n+m (x) = lim ϕ n lim ϕ m (x) = ϕ p ϕ q (x) .
                         n→p m→q                    n→p        m→q




Published: Graduate Text in Mathematics, vol. 272, Springer-Verlag, 2015.
382                                                             19 Topological Dynamics and Colorings

This shows that E is a semigroup and Φ is a homomorphism. To see continuity take
p ∈ βN, x ∈ K and U ⊆ K open with ϕ p (x) ∈ U. Choose f ∈ C(K; R) with 0 ≤ f ≤ 1
on K and f (ϕ p (x)) = 1, [ f > 0 ] ⊆ U. Then, by using Proposition 19.5,

                           f (ϕ q (x)) = lim f (ϕ n (x)) for all q ∈ βN.
                                           n→q

Whence, f (ϕ q (x)) > 0, i.e., ϕ q (x) ∈ U, whenever q is in an appropriate weak∗
neighborhood of p.

The semigroup E in the proposition above is called the enveloping semigroup or
Ellis semigroup of the topological system (K; ϕ). Here is another description.

Proposition 19.12. For a topological system (K; ϕ) define
                                         
                                     T := ϕ n : n ∈ N ⊆ K K ,

where the closure is understood in the topology of pointwise convergence of the
compact space K K (see Tychonoff’s Theorem A.5). Then T = E , the enveloping
semigroup.

Proof. For ψ ∈ T there is a net (nα ) with ϕ nα → ψ in K K . Since βN is compact,
(nα ) has a convergent subnet (nα 0 ) with limit p ∈ βN. By continuity of p 7→ ϕ p we
have ϕ p = ψ. On the other hand, if p ∈ βN, then there is a net (nα ) ⊆ N converging
to p. By compactness of T there a subnet (ϕ nα 0 ) with limit ψ ∈ T . By continuity
of p 7→ ϕ p we conclude ψ = ϕ p .

As a corollary we obtain the following.
Proposition 19.13. Let (K; ϕ) be a topological system.
    a) For x ∈ K                                  
                                       orb>0 (x) = ϕ p (x) : p ∈ βN .
   b) If (L; ϕ) is a subsystem, then L is invariant under ϕ p for every p ∈ βN.

Proof. a) Let T be as in Proposition 19.12. By compactness of T and by the con-
tinuity of point evaluations on K K the equality T x = {ψ(x) : ψ ∈ T } = orb>0 (x)
holds. Since E = T by Proposition 19.12, the assertion is proved.
b) follows from a).

   Given a topological system (K; ϕ) two points x, y ∈ K are called proximal (with
respect to the system) if there is a point z such that for every open neighborhood U
of z there is n ∈ N with
                                   ϕ n (x), ϕ n (y) ∈ U.
For metrizable spaces we have the following characterization.
Proposition 19.14. For a topological system (K; ϕ), K metrizable with metric d,
and for x, y ∈ K the following statements are equivalent:


Published: Graduate Text in Mathematics, vol. 272, Springer-Verlag, 2015.
19.3 Topological Dynamics Revisited                                                  383

   (i) x, y ∈ K are proximal.
  (ii) For every ε > 0 there is n ∈ N with d(ϕ n (x), ϕ n (y)) < ε.
 (iii) There is a subsequence (nk )k∈N in N such that

                                    d(ϕ nk (x), ϕ nk (y)) → 0         as k → ∞.

We leave the proof as Exercise 3. Being proximal is a symmetric and reflexive rela-
tion on K as it is easy to see. By a result of Ellis it is an equivalence relation if and
only if the enveloping semigroup E contains exactly one minimal right ideal, see
(Ellis 1960).
Proposition 19.15 (Idempotents and Proximal Points). Let (K; ϕ) be a topolog-
ical system. For x, y ∈ K the following assertions (i)–(iii) are equivalent:
   (i) The points x, y are proximal.
  (ii) There is p ∈ βN with
                                                 ϕ p (x) = ϕ p (y).
 (iii) There is an idempotent p ∈ βN (i.e., p2 = p) with

                                                 ϕ p (x) = ϕ p (y).

The next two assertions are equivalent and any one of them implies each of (i)–(iii):
 (iv) There is an idempotent p ∈ βN with ϕ p (x) = y.
  (v) There is p ∈ βN with ϕ p (x) = y and ϕ p (y) = y.
If the system (K; ϕ) is minimal, (i)–(v) are all equivalent.

Proof. (i) ⇒ (ii): Suppose x, y ∈ K are proximal points, and let z ∈ K be point as
in the definition of proximality. Then for every open neighborhood U of z we can
take the corresponding minimal nU ∈ N with ϕ nU (x), ϕ nU (y) ∈ U. By compactness
a subnet of (nU ) converges to some p ∈ βN (U ranging in a neighborhood basis),
and clearly ϕ p (x) = z = ϕ p (y).
(ii) ⇒ (iii): Define                 
                                 S := q ∈ βN : ϕ q (x) = ϕ q (y) .
By assumption S is nonempty, and it is compact by Proposition 19.11. Evidently S
is a subsemigroup of βN, hence by Ellis’ Theorem 16.3 contains an idempotent p.
(iii) ⇒ (i): Given p ∈ βN with ϕ p (x) = ϕ p (y) let U be an arbitrary open neighbor-
hood of z := ϕ p (x). Then by Proposition 19.11 there is n ∈ N with ϕ n (x), ϕ n (y) ∈ U.
(iv) ⇒ (v): Take an idempotent p ∈ βN as in (iv). Then y = ϕ p (x) = ϕ p ϕ p (x) =
ϕ p (y).
(v) ⇒ (iv): Consider the set
                          
                    S := q ∈ βN : ϕ q (x) = y and ϕ q (y) = y ,



Published: Graduate Text in Mathematics, vol. 272, Springer-Verlag, 2015.
384                                                             19 Topological Dynamics and Colorings

which is nonempty by assumption (v). By continuity of p 7→ ϕ p it is closed, hence
compact, and is evidently a subsemigroup. Therefore it contains an idempotent p ∈
βN.
The implication (v) ⇒ (ii) is trivial.
Suppose now that the system (K; ϕ) is minimal.
(ii) ⇒ (v): Let q ∈ βN be such that ϕ q (x) = ϕ q (y). By minimality orb>0 (ϕ q (x)) = K,
so by Proposition 19.13 there is u ∈ βN with ϕ u ϕ q (y) = ϕ u ϕ q (x) = y, i.e., p := u+q
is as asserted.

Theorem 19.16 (Auslander, Ellis). Let (K; ϕ) be a topological system. For x ∈ K
let L := orb>0 (x).
    a) Then for any subsystem (M; ϕ) of (L; ϕ) there is y ∈ M proximal to x.
   b) There is a uniformly recurrent point proximal to x.

Proof. a) Define                       
                                   S := p ∈ βN : ϕ p (x) ∈ M ,
which is nonempty by Proposition 19.13, and is a closed subset of βN by the defini-
tion of the topology of pointwise convergence and by the continuity of p 7→ ϕ p (x),
see Proposition 19.11. If z ∈ M, then z = ϕ q (x) for some q ∈ βN by Proposition
19.13, but then q ∈ S. We conclude M = {ϕ p (x) : p ∈ S}. For q ∈ βN, p ∈ S we have
ϕ p (x) ∈ M, ϕ q ϕ p (x) ∈ M by Proposition 19.13.b), so that βN + S ⊆ S, in particu-
lar S is a semigroup. By Theorem 16.3 it contains an idempotent u. By Proposition
19.15 y := ϕ u (x) ∈ M and x are proximal.
b) Take a minimal subsystem (M; ϕ) of (L; ϕ) (see Theorem 3.5). By Theorem 3.11
each point in M is uniformly recurrent. By part a) there is one which is proximal to
x.

   A topological system is called distal if every point is proximal only to itself.

In view of the previous list of examples it is interesting to note that Glasner (2006)
gives a characterization in terms of the enveloping semigroup of those minimal and
distal systems that are isometric (in a compatible metric), see also (Glasner 2007b).
Proposition 19.18 (Ellis). A topological system (K; ϕ) is distal if and only if its
enveloping semigroup E is a group.
Proof. Suppose that the enveloping semigroup is a group. Then the only idempo-
tent element in E is id : K → K, i.e., ϕ p = id for every idempotent p ∈ βN. By
Proposition 19.15 a point can be only proximal to itself.
Suppose (K; ϕ) is distal, and let ψ ∈ E be an idempotent. For x ∈ K set y := ψ(x),
then by Proposition 19.15 y and x are proximal, hence they must be equal by as-
sumption. This shows that ψ = id, i.e., the only idempotent in E is id. By Lemma
16.4 there is a minimal idempotent in E , which is then the only idempotent id.
Lemma 16.1 shows that E = id E id is a group.
As a consequence we obtain that a distal system is in fact invertible. Distal systems
have a simple “structure theorem” similarly to isometric systems, cf. Corollary 3.7,
see also Exercise 3.
Proposition 19.19. A distal topological system is a disjoint union of its minimal
subsystems.
Proof. By Theorem 19.16 every point x is proximal to a uniformly recurrent point z
in its orbit closure. By distality we must have x = z, hence every point is uniformly
recurrent, which proves the statement by Theorem 3.11 and Remark 3.2.4.
Furstenberg in (1963) proved a more detailed structure theorem for distal systems,
see also (Glasner 2003, Ch. 10).



19.4 Hindman’s Theorem

In this section we shall apply the foregoing results to one particular topological
system, namely the shift, and thereby arrive at a first result in combinatorial num-
ber theory. The following proposition describes proximality in the shift system (see
Example 2.5).


Published: Graduate Text in Mathematics, vol. 272, Springer-Verlag, 2015.
386                                                             19 Topological Dynamics and Colorings

Proposition 19.20. For given r ∈ N consider the shift system (Wr+ ; τ). Two points
x, y ∈ Wr+ are proximal if and only if the set
                             
                               n ∈ N0 : x(n) = y(n)

is thick, i.e., contains arbitrarily long blocks of consecutive integers.

Proof. By the definition of the topology on Wr+ for each compatible metric d on
Wr+ and every N ∈ N there is ε > 0 such that d(x, y) < ε if and only if the first
N letters of x and y coincide. This observation implies the assertion by Proposition
19.14.

Given an infinite sequence (n j ) j∈N in N we define
                            n                                 o
                 FS(n j ) := ∑ n j : F ⊆ N finite and nonempty ,
                                      j∈F

the set of nonempty finite sums of distinct members of the sequence. A finite se-
quence (n1 , . . . , nk ) ∈ Nk we complete by zeros to an infinite one and interpret
FS(n1 , . . . , nk ) accordingly. A set I containing FS(nk ) for some infinite sequence
(nk )k∈N in N is called an IP set.3
Remark 19.21. Some authors use the term IP set for sets that are of the form
FS(nk ), see, e.g., (Furstenberg 1981, Def. 2.3) and (Bergelson 2010).
Clearly, N and 2N are IP sets, while N \ 2N is not, see also Exercise 8.
Theorem 19.22 (Hindman, Arithmetic Version). If N = A1 ∪ A2 ∪ . . . ∪ Ar is a
partition, then there is j0 ∈ {1, . . . , r} such that A j0 is an IP set. More precisely,
there is a strictly increasing sequence (nk )k∈N in N such that FS(nk ) is contained in
A j0 .

Proof. Let N = A1 ∪ A2 ∪ · · · ∪ Ar be a partition. Consider the one-sided shift topo-
logical system (Wr+ ; τ) and define x ∈ Wr+ by x(0) := 1, and for n ∈ N by

                                         x(n) := j       if n ∈ A j .

Then by Theorem 19.16 there is a uniformly recurrent point z proximal to x. Set
j0 := z(0). We claim that A j0 has the asserted properties. For the proof, recall that
z ∈ Wr+ is uniformly recurrent if every finite block (word) that occurs in it, occurs
actually infinitely often with bounded gaps (i.e., syndetically, see Example 3.10.b)).
By Proposition 19.20 x and z are proximal if and only if x and z coincide on arbitrar-
ily large blocks occurring at the same position in x and z. Since every finite block of
z appears in every sufficiently large segment of z, it follows that every finite block
of z appears infinitely often somewhere at the same position in x and in z.

3 The terminology “IP” may refer to “Infinite Parallelepiped”. In fact, FS(n ) = {n , n , n +

n2 , n3 , n1 + n3 , n2 + n3 , n1 + n2 + n3 , . . . } resembles an infinite parallelepiped.

Consider the block b1 = ( j0 ) that occurs—by what is said above—in x and z at

first n1 + 1 letters of z. Also the block b2 occurs in x and z at the same position
n2 ∈ N with n2 > n1 . We therefore have

      z(0) = z(n2 ),                z(1) = z(n2 + 1),           ...              z(n1 ) = z(n2 + n1 ),
    x(n2 ) = z(n2 ),         x(n2 + 1) = z(n2 + 1),              ...        x(n2 + n1 ) = z(n2 + n1 ).

                              x(n1 + n2 ) = z(n1 + n2 ) = z(n1 ) = j0 ,

hence n1 , n2 , n1 +n2 ∈ A j0 . We continue this construction inductively. Suppose n1 <
n2 < · · · < nk have been found such that for any N ∈ FS(n1 , . . . , nk ) we have z(N) =

at the same position, say at nk+1 > nk both in x and z. This yields

                       z( j) = z(nk+1 + j),         for all j = 0, . . . , n1 + n2 + · · · nk ,
              z(nk+1 + j) = x(nk+1 + j) for all j = 0, . . . , n1 + n2 + · · · nk .

If N ∈ FS(n1 , . . . , nk ), then x(N + nk+1 ) = z(N + nk+1 ) = z(N), the latter being equal
to j0 by assumption. Thus we obtain N + nk+1 ∈ A j0 . Hence, by construction we
have FS(n j ) ⊆ A j0 .

We arrive at the following consequence of Hindman’s theorem.

Theorem 19.23 (Hindman, Set Theoretic Version). If F = A1 ∪ A2 ∪ . . . ∪ Ar is
a partition, then there is j0 ∈ {1, . . . , r} and a sequence (α j ) j∈N in F of pairwise
disjoint finite sets such that FU(α j ) ⊆ A j0 . The sequence (α j ) j∈N can be chosen
such that max α j < min α j+1 for all j ∈ N.

Proof. Identify N with the set of nonzero, finite 0-1-sequences via the binary ex-
pansion of n ∈ N, and in turn identify this latter set with F . That is we consider the
bijection
                         ι : F → N, ι(α) 7→ ∑ 2 j = n.
                                                               j∈α

The partition of F therefore induces a partition N = ι(A1 ) ∪ . . . ∪ ι(Ar ). Hindman’s
Theorem 19.22 yields a strictly increasing sequence (nk )k∈N with FS(nk ) ⊆ ι(A j0 )
for some j0 ∈ {1, . . . , r}. The proof will be finished if we find a subsequence (n0k )k∈N
in FS(nk ) such that ι −1 (n0k ) are pairwise disjoint for k ∈ N and FS(n0k ) ⊆ FS(nk ).

Indeed, in that case α j := ι −1 (n0j ), j ∈ N, have the asserted properties, because
ι(α j ∪ α j0 ) = ι(α j ) + ι(α j0 ).
To construct the required sequence we first show that for every finite set N ⊆ F
and for every K ∈ N there is m ∈ FS(nk ) such that β ∩ ι −1 (m) = /0 for all β ∈ N and
such that m is the sum of elements n j with j > K. This assertion is trivial if there are
only finitely many members of (nk )k∈N that intersect some element β of N . So we
can suppose that this happens for infinitely many of the members. Let N be greater
than the maximum of any element of any β ∈ N . Then for infinitely many members
of (nk )k∈N we have nk ≡ constant modulo 2N , i.e., that ι −1 (nk ) ∩ {0, . . . , N} = γ for
some γ. We add up 2N of such nk with k > K, the result m then belongs to FS(nk )
and has the asserted properties.
Let now n01 = n1 , and suppose n01 , . . . , n0k ∈ FS(nk ) have been defined. Let N :=
{ι −1 (n0j ) : j = 1, . . . , k} and let K ∈ N be greater than the index j of elements n j
that occur in the sums giving n01 , . . . , n0k . Take m ∈ FS(nk ) as above and set n0k+1 := m.
By construction we have FS(n0k ) ⊆ FS(nk ) and (n0k )k∈N is as required. Note also that
the construction yields (α j ) j∈N with the asserted additional property.

   A subset A ⊆ N is called an IP∗ set if it intersects every IP set. Trivially, N is
an IP∗ set. In some sense IP∗ sets are large (near infinity). In fact, an IP set may
contain arbitrarily growing gaps, so a set intersecting any such set must be indeed
“large near infinity”. By Exercise 14 an IP∗ set is syndetic (i.e., has bounded gaps).
If I ∗ ⊆ N is an IP∗ set, then N = I ∗ ∪ I ∗ c is a partition, hence by the arithmetic
version of Hindman’s theorem, I ∗ is an IP set. See also Exercise 21.
Corollary 19.24.    a) Let I ⊆ N be an IP set and let I = A1 ∪ A2 ∪ · · · ∪ Ar be a
      partition. Then there is j0 ∈ {1, . . . , r} such that A j0 is an IP set.
   b) If I ∗ and J ∗ are IP∗ sets, so is I ∗ ∩ J ∗ .

Proof. a) Let (nk )k∈N be a sequence in N with FS(nk ) ⊆ I. For j = 1, . . . , r we define
                                    n                o
                              A j := α : ∑ nk ∈ A j .
                                                      k∈α

Then F = A1 ∪ · · · ∪ Ar , and Hindman’s Theorem 19.23 yields (αk )k∈N pairwise
disjoint with FU(αk ) ⊆ A j0 for some j0 . Then with mk := ι(αk ) we have FS(mk ) ⊆
A j0 , i.e., A j0 is an IP set, where ι is as in the proof of Theorem 19.23.
b) Let I ∗ and J ∗ be IP∗ sets, and let I be an IP set. Then I = (I \ I ∗ ) ∪ (I ∩ I ∗ ) is a
partition, hence by part a) one of the sets contains an IP set, but since I ∗ is an IP∗
set, this cannot hold for I \ I ∗ . Hence, there is an IP set J ⊆ I ∩ I ∗ , which is then
intersected by J ∗ . This shows that I ∗ ∩ J ∗ intersects any IP set I, i.e., I ∗ ∩ J ∗ is an IP∗
set.

19.5 From Coloring to Recurrence Results

In this section we give a proof of van der Waerden’s theorem on arithmetic progres-
sions using directly the semigroup βN. Then we show how topological recurrence
results can be deduced from this theorem.

Theorem 19.25 (Van der Waerden). Let

                            N = A1 ∪ A2 ∪ . . . ∪ Ar         for some r ∈ N.

Then there is j0 ∈ {1, . . . , r} such that A j0 contains arithmetic progressions of arbi-
trary length, i.e., for all k ∈ N there are a, n ∈ N such that

                             a, a + n, a + 2n, . . . , a + (k − 1)n ∈ A j0 .

We prepare the proof by defining the sets
        
  Ik := (a, a + n, a + 2n, . . . , a + (k − 1)n) : a ∈ N, n ∈ N ⊆ N × N × · · · × N

for all k ∈ N. A set A ⊆ N contains a k-term arithmetic progression if and only if

                                       Ik ∩ A × A × · · · × A 6= /0.

In order to have compact spaces we consider the k-fold product

                                   (βN)k = βN × βN × · · · × βN,

which is a right-topological semigroup with the coordinatewise operation and the
product topology. The closure Ik of Ik is a compact set in (βN)k . Clearly, Ik is a
subsemigroup, and if we take the smaller semigroup
             
      Sk := (a, a + n, a + 2n, . . . , a + (k − 1)n) : a ∈ N, n ∈ N0 ⊆ (βN)k ,

then Ik becomes an ideal in Sk . We next prove a general result about right-topological
semigroups.
Proposition 19.26. Let S be subsemigroup in a compact right-topological semi-
group H such that the left multiplications by elements from S are continuous, and
let I be a two-sided ideal in S. Then S is a compact right-topological subsemigroup
of H, and I is a two-sided ideal of S.

Proof. Compactness of S and the continuity of right multiplications is clear. To
show that S is a semigroup take x, y ∈ S and W an open neighborhood of xy. By the
continuity of the right multiplication by y there is an open neighborhood V of x with
V y ⊆ W . Take z ∈ V ∩ S. By the continuity of the left multiplication by z, there is an
open neighborhood U of y with zU ⊆ W . For w ∈ U ∩ S we have wz ∈ W ∩ S. This
proves xy ∈ S. The arguments to show that I is an ideal in S are similar.



Published: Graduate Text in Mathematics, vol. 272, Springer-Verlag, 2015.
390                                                             19 Topological Dynamics and Colorings

By this proposition Sk is a right-topological subsemigroup in (βN)k , and Ik is a
two-sided ideal of Sk . In the search for a k-term arithmetic progression in A ⊆ N it
suffices to show that for the set
                                   
                             A∗ := p ∈ βN : p(1A ) = 1

one has
                                     Ik ∩ A∗ × A∗ × · · · × A∗ 6= /0.
Indeed, the set A∗ is open since by Lemma 19.6 we have
                                  
                            A∗ = p ∈ βN : p(1A ) 6= 0 .

Hence, the product set A∗ × A∗ × · · · × A∗ is open in (βN)k . So if it intersects Ik , then
for some a, n ∈ N one has

                       (a, a + n, . . . , a + (k − 1)n) ∈ A∗ × A∗ × · · · × A∗ ,
meaning that             a, a + n, . . . , a + (k − 1)n ∈ A.

We therefore try to find elements of Ik .
Theorem 19.27. Let p ∈ βN be contained in a minimal right ideal of βN. Then

                                           (p, p, . . . , p) ∈ Ik .

Proof. Notice first that (p, p, . . . , p) ∈ Sk . Since by Proposition 19.26 Ik is a two-
sided ideal, by Lemma 16.4 it is enough to show that (p, p, . . . , p) is contained in
a minimal right ideal. Let R be a minimal right ideal containing p, which exists
by assumption. Since the right ideal R × R × · · · × R is not minimal in general, we
need the following considerations. Of course, (p, . . . , p) + Sk is a right ideal in Sk ,
hence contains a minimal right ideal J. This right ideal is itself a compact right-
topological semigroup, so contains an idempotent element (q1 , q2 , . . . , qk ) by Ellis’
Theorem 16.3. By construction there is (u1 , u2 , . . . , uk ) ∈ Sk with

                                    p + ui = qi       for i = 1, . . . , k.

Hence, from p ∈ R we obtain qi ∈ R since R is a right ideal. Thus qi + βN ⊆ R and
by minimality of R even the equality qi + βN = R is true. For some elements q0i ∈ βN
one has qi + q0i = p and then

                                qi + p = qi + qi + q0i = qi + q0i = p.

To conclude the proof notice that

                      (p, . . . , p) = (q1 , . . . , qk ) + (p, . . . , p) ∈ J + S = J,

so (p, . . . , p) is contained in a minimal right ideal.

Proof of van der Waerden’s Theorem 19.25. Notice that it suffices to prove that for
every k ∈ N there is a j0 (k) ∈ {1, . . . , r} with A j0 (k) containing a k-term arithmetic
progression. Indeed, we have j0 (k) = j0 for some j0 ∈ {1, . . . , r} and for infinitely
many k ∈ N. This j0 will serve our purposes.
By Theorem 16.3 there is a minimal right ideal R in βN. Take p ∈ R. From Theorem
19.27 we obtain (p, p, . . . , p) ∈ Ik . By Lemma 19.6.c) p(1A j0 ) = 1 for some j0 ∈
{1, . . . , r}, i.e., p ∈ A∗j0 . Whence it follows that

                                   Ik ∩ A∗j0 × A∗j0 × · · · × A∗j0 6= /0,

proving that A j0 contains a k-term arithmetic progression.
   We show how to deduce recurrence results from combinatorial ones. Recall
Birkhoff’s recurrence theorem from Chapter 3: In any metric topological system
(K; ϕ) there is point x0 ∈ K which is recurrent, meaning that ϕ n j (x0 ) → x0 as j → ∞
for a subsequence (n j ) j∈N in N. We now search for a point x0 which enjoys even
stronger recurrence properties, such as

                      ϕ n j (x0 ) → x0      and     ϕ 2n j (x0 ) → x0       as j → ∞.

We saw in Exercise 11 that any point x0 that is recurrent for ϕ is also recurrent for
ϕ 2 (actually for every ϕ m , m ∈ N). So there are subsequences (n j ) j∈N and (n0j ) j∈N
in N such that
                                                         0
                      ϕ n j (x0 ) → x0      and     ϕ 2n j (x0 ) → x0       as j → ∞.

But nothing prevents these subsequences from being disjoint. However, we shall
derive the existence of such an x0 from van der Waerden’s theorem.

Remark 19.34. Let S be the semigroup generated by the transformations
ϕ1 , . . . , ϕk . Lemma 19.32 and Theorem 19.31 imply that if the action of S is mini-
mal on K, then for every nonempty open set V we have

                               V ∩ ϕ1−nV ∩ ϕ2−nV ∩ · · · ∩ ϕk−nV 6= /0.

Even more, the set
                        
                    A := n ∈ N : V ∩ ϕ1−nV ∩ ϕ2−nV ∩ · · · ∩ ϕk−nV 6= /0

intersects an arbitrary IP set I nontrivially, i.e., it is an IP∗ set. By Exercise 14 an
IP∗ set is syndetic, so that we see that the set A of simultaneous return times for
ϕ1 , . . . , ϕk has bounded gaps. Compare this with Birkhoff’s Theorem 3.14.

    We conclude this chapter by showing how to obtain combinatorial results from
topological ones, thereby putting the last color (in this book) to the landscape
of topological dynamics and combinatorics. Rado (1943) attributes the following
multi-dimensional van der Waerden type result to Gallai. It was Witt who gave the
first published proof in (Witt 1952). Using the result of Furstenberg and Weiss a
proof is readily at hand.

Notes and Further Reading

Van der Waerden’s theorem solves a conjecture of Baudet and was published in (van
der Waerden 1927), see also van der Waerden (1971), (1998). Our proof in Sec-
tion 19.5 is from (Todorcevic 1997, Ch. 2). The Stone–Čech compactification can
be constructed for every completely regular topological space X via the universal
property described in Proposition 19.4 and Exercise 1, see, e.g., (Willard 2004, Sec.
19). This compactification βX is the Gelfand representation space of the C∗ -algebra
Cb (X) of bounded and continuous function over X. Our treatment of βS follows this
route, in contrast to the more standard way in topological dynamics of utilizing ul-
trafilters. See (Haase 1997) for a detailed account on the various approaches to βN
and for applications in topological dynamics. A standard reference on the semigroup
βS is (Hindman and Strauss 1998), where the notions introduced in this chapter are
studied systematically in the utmost detail. The enveloping semigroup goes back
to Ellis (1960) and to Ellis and Gottschalk (1960), see also (Glasner 2007a). Ellis
(1958) proved Proposition 19.18 for general group actions, and the proof we pre-
sented carries over for the case of semigroups actions as well.
Theorem 19.16 is due to Auslander (1960) and Ellis (1960). The notion of distality
can be traced back to Hilbert (1902) where he attempts the foundation of plane
geometry via axiomatizing rigid motions, see the discussion after his Axiom III in
(Hilbert 1902). Distal dynamical systems gained considerable attention during the
years, see (Gottschalk and Hedlund 1955), culminating in the famous Furstenberg
structure theorem for distal systems, see (Furstenberg 1963). The attention was even
intensified after the tight connection to combinatorics was discovered.
Hindman’s theorem appeared in (Hindman 1974) the presented proof is due to
Furstenberg and Weiss (1978b). The results of Section 19.3 were taken from
Furstenberg’s book (Furstenberg 1981, Ch. 8), but there are a number of other
sources that were helpful, among which Bergelson’s papers (1987), (1996), (2000)
and (2010) were the most inspiring. For more on this circle of ideas, for extensions
we refer to these papers and the references therein.
The proof of Theorem 19.31 is extracted from two papers by Bergelson and by
Leibman. They proved that the multiple recurrence theorem remains valid even if
                                              p (n)          p (n)
the powers ϕ1n , . . . , ϕkn are replaced by ϕ1 1 , . . . , ϕk k for some integer polyno-
mials, see (Bergelson and Leibman 1996). Further, instead of commutativity of the
transformations it suffices to suppose that the homeomorphisms ϕ1 , . . . , ϕk generate
a nilpotent group, see (Leibman 1994). However, the core of the presented proof
goes back to the seminal paper (Furstenberg and Weiss 1978b).
The first published proof of the Gallai–Witt theorem was by Witt (1952). However,
according to Rado (1943), Gallai (Grünwald) had his proof for this beautiful result



Published: Graduate Text in Mathematics, vol. 272, Springer-Verlag, 2015.
398                                                             19 Topological Dynamics and Colorings

some 20 years before. Section 42 of (Soifer 2009) contains historical information
on the Gallai–Witt theorem together with a combinatorial proof.



Exercises

1. Let S be a nonempty set (with the discrete topology) and let K, L be compact
spaces with the property that for an arbitrary compact space M any (continuous)
function f : S → M factorizes through both K and L. Prove that K and L are home-
omorphic and that S is homeomorphic to a topological subspace of K and L. A
compact space K with the above property is called the Stone–Čech compactifica-
tion of the discrete space S, which we see, by virtue of this exercise, to be unique
up to homeomorphisms.

       semigroups.
   d) βN is noncommutative, and not left-topological.

Arithmetic Progressions and Ergodic Theory




   If I have seen less than other men, it is because I have walked in the footsteps of giants.
                                                                                Paul R. Chernoff

In Chapter 19 we saw van der Waerden’s theorem (1927) as an application of topo-
logical dynamics: If we color the natural numbers with finitely many colors, then
we find arbitrarily long monochromatic arithmetic progressions, i.e., progressions
all of whose members carry the same color.
    Many years later, a major extension of this result was proved by Szemerédi
(1975) using the concept of the upper density

                                               card(A ∩ {1, . . . , n})
                            d(A) := lim sup
                                        n→∞             n

of a subset A ⊆ N (in connection with the upper density see also Section 9.2, Exer-
cises 9.4 and 9.5).

Theorem 20.1 (Szemerédi). Any subset A ⊆ N with d(A) > 0 is AP-rich, i.e.,
contains arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions.

Recall that by Exercise 9.5 van der Waerden’s theorem is indeed a consequence of
this: If N = A1 ∪ · · · ∪ Ar , r ∈ N, then d(A j0 ) > 0 for at least one j0 ∈ {1, . . . , r}.
   Furstenberg and Weiss showed how to deduce number theoretic statements like
van der Waerden’s and Hindman’s theorems from multiple recurrence properties of
topological dynamical systems. The forerunner for this was a ground-breaking dis-
covery of Furstenberg who transferred Szemerédi’s theorem to a multiple recurrence
statement about measure theoretic dynamical systems giving an alternative proof of
Szemerédi’s theorem relying on ergodic theory.
   Furstenberg ideas—building heavily on the structure theory of ergodic measure-
preserving systems—were further developed by many authors and finally led to one
of the most striking results in this area so far.

Theorem 20.2 (Green–Tao). The set P of prime numbers is AP-rich.


                                                                                                 403
404                                                    20 Arithmetic Progressions and Ergodic Theory

We refer to (Green and Tao 2008) and in particular to Tao’s ICM lecture (2007)
and (Kra 2007) for the connection with ergodic theory. Newer developments in
this direction concerning patterns in the set of primes can be found in (Green and
Tao 2010a), (Tao and Ziegler 2008) and (Tao and Ziegler 2013).
   The discovery of such a beautiful structure within the chaos of prime numbers
was preceded and accompanied by various numerical experiments. Starting from
the arithmetic progression 7, 37, 67, 97, 127, 157 (of length 6 and difference 30) the
actual world record (smallest difference, as of November, 2014) by Fry1 is a pro-
gression of length 26 starting at

                                       3 486 107 472 997 423

with difference
                                        371 891 575 525 470.


   However striking, the Green–Tao theorem still falls short of the following auda-
cious conjecture formulated by Erdős and Turán in 1936, cf. Exercise 1.

Conjecture 20.3 (Erdős–Turán). Let A ⊆ N be such that ∑a∈A (1/a) = ∞. Then A
is AP-rich.

   The Green–Tao theorem is—even in its ergodic theoretic parts—beyond the
scope of this book. However, we shall describe the major link between “density
results” (like Szemerédi’s) and ergodic theory and apply it to obtain weaker, but
nevertheless stunning results (the theorems of Roth and Furstenberg–Sárközy). Our
major operator theoretic tool will be the JdLG-decomposition.



20.1 From Ergodic Theory to Arithmetic Progressions

We first translate assertions about arithmetic progressions to the language of ergodic
theory. Let us fix a subset A ⊆ N with positive upper density d(A) > 0. For given
k ∈ N consider the following statement.

       There exist a, n ∈ N such that a, a + n, a + 2n, . . . a + (k − 1)n ∈ A.              (APk )

Our goal is to construct an associated dynamical system that allows us to reformu-
late (APk ) in ergodic theoretic terms. This construction is known as Furstenberg’s
correspondence principle.
   Consider the compact metric space W2+ = {0, 1}N0 and the left shift τ on it. A
subset B ⊆ N0 can be identified with a point in W2+ via its characteristic function:

In (Furstenberg 1977) it was shown that (20.5) is indeed true for every ergodic
measure-preserving system and every k ∈ N. This completed the ergodic theoretic
proof of Szemerédi’s theorem. As a matter of fact, Furstenberg proved the truth of
the seemingly stronger version

of (20.5) As we shall see in a moment, this makes no difference because, actually,
the limit exists.



20.2 Back from Arithmetic Progressions to Ergodic Theory

We have seen how to obtain Szemerédi’s theorem from ergodic theoretic results. In
this section, we go in the opposite direction and show how to deduce statements
about measure-preserving systems from Szemerédi’s theorem.
    First of all we need a finitary reformulation of Szemerédi’s theorem, in analogy
to the finitary version of Gallai’s Theorem 19.36. We deduce it from Theorem 20.1,
while the converse implication is direct, see Exercise 2.

Theorem 20.5 (Szemerédi, Finitary Version). For every ε > 0 and k ∈ N, k ≥ 2
there is N = N(ε, k) such that whenever A ⊆ N is contained in an interval of length
` ≥ N and card(A) ≥ ε`, then A contains a k-term arithmetic progression.

Proof. Suppose by contradiction that the statement is false, i.e., that there is ε > 0
and k ∈ N such that for every N there is AN ⊆ N without k-term arithmetic pro-

card(A) ≥ `ε. This indirect assumption for N = 1 yields `1 and A1 ⊆ [1, `1 ] with-

shifting the sets, we find intervals I j = [a j , b j ] of length ` j = b j − a j + 1 such that for
every j ∈ N we have ` j+1 > b j and the gap g j := a j+1 − b j − 1 between I j and I j+1
equals b j + ` j+1 , and such that each I j contains a set A j with card(A j ) ≥ ε` j ≥ ε j
but without k-term arithmetic progressions. If we set

The Host–Kra Theorem for k = 3

The proof is based on the foregoing particular cases. Our major tool is the JdLG-

Some Ideas behind the Proof for k ≥ 4

We very briefly present the general strategy to prove Theorem 20.14 and high-
light some of the main ideas. First we recall some facts about factors of measure-
preserving systems (see Chapters 13 and 17). Let X = (X, Σ , µ) and Y = (Y, Σ 0 , ν)
be probability spaces and let (X; ϕ) and (Y; ψ) be measure-preserving systems with
Koopman operators T := Tϕ and S := Tψ , respectively. The system (Y; ψ) is called a
factor of (X; ϕ) if there is a Markov embedding R : L1 (Y) → L1 (X) intertwining the
Koopman operators, i.e., with T R = RS. In this case, (X; ϕ) is called an extension
of (Y; ψ). The range F := ran(R) of R is a unital Banach sublattice of L1 (X) and is
the range of the Markov projection Q = RR0 . Moreover, there is a sub-σ -algebra ΣF
with F = L1 (X, ΣF , µ), and we have

                         Q f = E( f | ΣF ) the conditional expectation.

invertible extension, which is ergodic if the original system was ergodic. Exercise
16 yields that it suffices to prove the Host–Kra theorem for invertible systems.

For k = 2, the fixed factor is characteristic for 1-term averages as we saw in the
proof of von Neumann’s Theorem 8.1. On the other hand, Lemma 20.18 shows that
the Kronecker factor Erev is characteristic for 2-term averages, and it was simple
to compute the averages for functions coming from this factor. Note that in general
the Kronecker factor is not characteristic for (k − 1)-term everages for k ≥ 4, see
Exercise 15.
   For k ≥ 4, the philosophy remains the same: One looks for a characteristic factor
with enough structure such that the limit of the averages (20.15) can be computed
whenever all functions are from this characteristic factor. In general, however, the
characteristic factors are considerably more complicated than the Kronecker factor.

averages, and it is sometimes called the universal characteristic factor. The main
difficulty is to find enough structure for these factors. One can show that the factors
(Zd−1 ; θd−1 ) come from homogeneous systems G/Γ for a (d − 1)-step nilpotent
group G and a discrete cocompact subgroup Γ of G rather than from rotations on
compact Abelian groups as for the Kronecker factor. For such systems, (even point-
wise) convergence of multiple ergodic averages had been known for some time,
so the Host–Kra theorem could be proved this way. We refer to (Parry 1969b),
(Parry 1970), (Lesigne 1991), (Host and Kra 2005b) and (Kra 2007) for details.
The above construction of the uniformity seminorms and their equivalent geometric
characterization due to Host and Kra (2005b) goes back to Gowers (2001) who
used analogous seminorms on finite Abelian groups in his Fourier analytic proof
of Szemerédi’s theorem. For further properties of the Gowers–Host–Kra seminorms
see (Eisner and Tao 2012).

Sketch of the Proof of Furstenberg’s Theorem for k ≥ 4

The above proof of convergence and recurrence for k = 3 is due to Furstenberg
(1977). The case k ≥ 4 is substantially more complicated. There are several er-
godic theoretic proofs of Szemerédi’s theorem: the original one from (Fursten-
berg 1977) using diagonal measures, one using characteristic factors due to Fursten-
berg, Katznelson, Ornstein (1982), one using the construction in the proof of Host
and Kra, see (Bergelson et al. 2008). There are also several further proofs using
tools from other areas such as “higher-order” Fourier analysis, see Gowers (2001),
model theory, see Towsner (2010), hypergraphs, see Gowers (2007), Tao (2006),
Nagle, Rödl, Schlacht (2006), Schlacht, Skokan (2004), and more, see, e.g., Green,
Tao (2010b). Thus the fascinating story of finding alternative proofs of Szemerédi’s
theorem seems not to be finished yet.
   We now sketch very briefly the proof due to Furstenberg, Katznelson, Ornstein
(1982), and for details we refer to (Furstenberg 1981, Ch. 7), (Petersen 1989, Sec.
4.3), (Tao 2009, Ch. 2), or (Einsiedler and Ward 2011, Ch. 7).
If (Y; ψ)
        R
           is the trivial factor,
                             R
                                  i.e., ΣY = { /0,Y }, then the corresponding projection is
Q f = Y f , L1 (Y) = C1, Y c1 = c. By Theorem 17.19 a measure-preserving system
(X; ϕ) is weakly mixing if and only if its Kronecker factor is trivial, and if and only
if it has no nontrivial compact factors (i.e., factors that are isomorphic to a compact
Abelian group rotation).
We say that a measure-preserving system (X; ϕ) has the SZ-property (SZ for Sze-
merédi) if for every k ≥ 2 and every f ∈ L∞ (X) with f > 0 (20.11) holds. Theo-
rem 20.19 thus expresses that each ergodic measure-preserving system has the SZ-
property. By Proposition 20.15 we know that weakly mixing systems do have the
SZ-property, and so do systems with discrete spectrum by Exercise 3.
To prove Furstenberg’s theorem, one needs relativized versions of the notions “weak
mixing” and “discrete spectrum”. Let (X; ϕ), (Y; ψ) be measure-preserving systems
with Koopman operators T and S respectively, and suppose (Y; ψ) is a factor of
(X; ϕ) with the associated Markov projection Q ∈ M(X; Y). We call (X; ϕ) weakly
mixing relative to (Y; ψ), or a relatively weakly mixing extension of (Y; ψ) if
                                        Z
                              1 N
                          lim
                          N→∞ N
                                ∑ Y |Q(T n f · g) − Sn Q f · Qg|2 = 0
                                n=1

holds for every f , g ∈ L∞ (X). For the trivial factor (Y; ψ) this means

                               1 N
                            lim
                           N→∞ N
                                 ∑ |hT n f , gi − h f , 1i · h1, gi|2 = 0,
                                 n=1

i.e., weak mixing by Theorem 9.19 (and Remark 9.20). One can prove the following
result:
   1) Suppose (Y; ψ) has the SZ-property and (X; ϕ) is a relatively weakly mixing
      extension of (Y; ψ), then also (X; ϕ) has the SZ-property.


Published: Graduate Text in Mathematics, vol. 272, Springer-Verlag, 2015.
20.5 The Furstenberg–Sárközy Theorem                                                423

The proof uses the van der Corput lemma and is almost literally the same as for
Proposition 20.15.
Another notion needed is that of compact extensions which can be defined in purely
measure theoretic terms. We shall not give the definition here but note that for the
proof of Furstenberg’s theorem only the following two properties of compact exten-
sions are needed:
   2) If (X; ϕ) is a not relatively weakly mixing extension of (Y; ψ), then there
      is an intermediate factor (Z; θ ) of (X; ϕ) which is a compact extension of
      (Y; ψ).
   3) If (Z; θ ) is a compact extension of (Y; ψ) and (Y; ψ) has the SZ-property,
      then so does (Z; θ ).
Consider now the set F of all factors with the SZ-property which is nonempty
since it contains the trivial factor. The set F can be partially ordered by the relation
of “being a factor”. By an argument using Zorn’s lemma, after checking the chain
condition, one finds a maximal element (Y; ψ) in F . If (X; ϕ) is a weakly mixing
extension of (Y; ψ), then by 1) above also (X; ϕ) has the SZ-property. Otherwise, by
2), there is a compact extension (Z; θ ) of (Y; ψ), which by 3) has the SZ-property,
contradicting maximality.



20.5 The Furstenberg–Sárközy Theorem

We continue in the same spirit, but instead of arithmetic progressions we now
look for pairs of the form {a, a + n2 } for a, n ∈ N, see (Furstenberg 1977),
(Sárközy 1978a).

Theorem 20.21 (Furstenberg–Sárközy). If A ⊆ N has positive upper density,
then there exist a, n ∈ N such that a, a + n2 ∈ A.

In order to prove the above theorem we first need an appropriate correspondence
principle.

Theorem 20.22 (Furstenberg Correspondence Principle for Squares). If for
every ergodic measure-preserving system (X; ϕ), its Koopman operator T := Tϕ on
L2 (X) and every 0 < f ∈ L∞ (X) there exists n ∈ N such that the condition
                                           Z
                                                        2
                                                 f · (T n f ) > 0               (20.18)
                                             X

is satisfied, then Theorem 20.21 holds.

The proof of this correspondence principle is analogous to the one of Theorem 20.4.
Then, to prove Theorem 20.21 one first shows that for a measure-preserving system
(X; ϕ) and its Koopman operator T := Tϕ the limit


Published: Graduate Text in Mathematics, vol. 272, Springer-Verlag, 2015.
424                                                    20 Arithmetic Progressions and Ergodic Theory

                                              1 N
                                                ∑ f ·Tn f
                                                       2
                                           lim                                              (20.19)
                                          N→∞ N
                                                n=1

exists in L2 (X) for every f ∈ L∞ (X), see Theorem 21.17 below for a more general
case. So to conclude the proof of Theorem 20.21 it remains to prove the following.

Proposition 20.23. Let (X; ϕ) be an ergodic measure-preserving system. Then the
limit (20.19) is strictly positive for every 0 < f ∈ L∞ (X).

The proof is analogous to that of Theorem 20.19 for k = 3 and again uses the de-
composition L2 (X) = Eaws ⊕ Erev , the vanishing of the above limit on Eaws and a
relative denseness argument on Erev , see Exercise 4.
A sequence (nk )k∈N is called a Poincaré sequence (see, e.g., Def. 3.6 in (Fursten-
berg 1981)) if for every measure-preserving system (X; ϕ), X = (X, Σ , µ), and A ∈ Σ
with µ(A) > 0 one has
                                      
                       µ A ∩ ϕ −nk (A) > 0 for some k ∈ N.

In this case the set {nk : k ∈ N} is called a set of recurrence. Poincaré’s Theorem
6.13 tells that (n)n∈N is a Poincaré sequence, explaining the terminology. One can
prove that Proposition 20.23 remains valid even for not necessarily ergodic measure-
preserving systems, so we obtain that (n2 )n∈N is a Poincaré sequence. More gener-
ally, we will see in the next chapter that (p(n))n∈N is a Poincaré sequence for every
integer polynomial p with p(0) = 0, see also Exercise 17.
Furthermore, Sárközy (1978b) showed that Theorem 20.21 also remains valid if one
replaces the set of differences {n2 : n ∈ N} by the shifted set of primes P − 1, i.e.,
if A has positive upper density then there are a ∈ N, p ∈ P with a, a + p − 1 ∈ A.
As in the case of arithmetic progressions handled earlier in this chapter, one can
establish a Furstenberg correspondence principle in both directions and show that
Sárközy’s result is equivalent to the statement that P − 1 is a set of recurrence. For
more examples of sets of recurrence such as P + 1 and sets coming from generalized
polynomials as well as properties and related notions see, e.g., (Bourgain 1987),
(Bergelson and Håland 1996), (Bergelson et al. 2014).
Host and Kra (2005a) proved convergence of multiple ergodic averages for totally
ergodic systems with powers p1 (n), . . . , pk−1 (n) replacing n, . . . , (k − 1)n in (20.12):

                        1 N                                                
                     lim
                    N→∞ N
                          ∑   T p1 (n) f1 · T p2 (n) f2 · · · T pk−1 (n) fk−1 ,
                          n=1

where p1 , . . . , pk−1 are arbitrary polynomials with integer coefficients. Leibman
(2005a) tackled the case of general ergodic systems. With an additional assump-
tion p j (0) = 0 for every j ∈ {1, . . . , k − 1}, this leads to an alternative proof of the
so-called polynomial Szemerédi theorem, i.e., the existence of a subset of the form
{a, a + p1 (n), . . . , a + pk−1 (n)} in every set A ⊆ N with positive upper density. This


Published: Graduate Text in Mathematics, vol. 272, Springer-Verlag, 2015.
Exercises                                                                          425

has been proved originally in (Bergelson and Leibman 1996), but see (Bergelson et
al. 2008) for details and for the weakest possible assumption on the polynomials.
The results of Szemerédi and Furstenberg–Sárközy presented in this chapter remain
true in a slightly strengthened form. One can replace the upper density d by the
so-called upper Banach density defined as

                                              card(A ∩ {m, . . . , m + n})
                           Bd(A) := lim sup                                ,
                                        m,n→∞           n+1

while the lower Banach density Bd(A) is defined analogously by the lim inf. The
actual change to be carried out in order to obtain these generalizations is in Fursten-
berg’s correspondence principle(s), see (Furstenberg 1981) and Exercise 5.
   Banach densities and Banach limits (see Exercise 10.3) are intrinsically con-
nected: By (Jerison 1957) the upper Banach density of A ⊆ N is the supremum of
the values of Banach limits on 1A , and in turn, the lower Banach density is given by
the infimum of all these values.

More Ergodic Theorems




   Jede wahre Geschichte ist eine unendliche Geschichte.1
                                                                        Michael Ende2

As we saw in previous chapters, ergodic theorems, even though being originally
motivated by a recurrence question from physics, found applications in unexpected
areas such as number theory. So it is not surprising that they attracted continuous at-
tention among the mathematical community, thus leading to various generalizations
and extensions. In this chapter we describe a very few of them.



21.1 Weighted Ergodic Theorems

As a first generalization we study convergence of weighted ergodic averages and
characterize weights which are “good” for the mean ergodic theorem.

Definition 21.1. A sequence (an )n∈N in C is called a (universally) good weight for
the mean ergodic theorem if for every Hilbert space H and every linear contraction
T on H, the weighted averages

                                                     1 N
                                AN,(an ) [T ] f :=     ∑ an T n f
                                                     N n=1
                                                                                   (21.1)

converge for every f ∈ H as N → ∞.

The following is a surprisingly simple criterion for a sequence to be good in the
previous sense, see, e.g., (Berend et al. 2002).


1 Every real story is a Neverending Story.
2 Die unendliche Geschichte, Thienemann Verlag, 2012 · Translation from: Michael Ende, The

Neverending Story, translated by Ralph Mannheim, Puffin Books, 1983.

430                                                                         21 More Ergodic Theorems

Theorem 21.2. For a bounded sequence (an )n∈N in C the following assertions are
equivalent:
   (i) The sequence (an )n∈N is a good weight for the mean ergodic theorem.
  (ii) For every isometry T on a Hilbert space H the weighted averages AN,(an ) [T ] f
       converge strongly for every f ∈ H.
 (iii) For every isometry T on a Hilbert space H the weighted averages
       AN,(an ) [T ] f converge weakly for every f ∈ H.
 (iv) The limit
                                               1 N
                                            lim
                                           N→∞ N
                                                 ∑ an λ n =: c(λ )                            (21.2)
                                                 n=1

         exists for every λ ∈ T.
In this case, for every contraction T ∈ L (H) one has

                                         1 N
            lim AN,(an ) [T ] f = lim
           N→∞                       N→∞ N
                                           ∑ an T n f = ∑ c(λ )Pλ f ,                         (21.3)
                                           n=1         λ ∈σ (T )∩T    p


where the operators Pλ are the orthogonal projections onto the mutually orthogonal
eigenspaces ker(T − λ I) for λ ∈ σp (T ) ∩ T.

Proof. First of all we note that the sum on the right-hand side of (21.3) is strongly
convergent for every bounded function c : T → C, because by Exercise 16.19 eigen-
vectors of a contraction to different unimodular eigenvalues are orthogonal.
The implications (i) ⇒ (ii) ⇒ (iii) are trivial, and (iii) ⇒ (iv) follows by considering
the multiplication by λ as an operator on H = C.
Now, we show that for an isometry T one has AN,(an ) [T ] f → 0 for every f ∈ Haws .
For f ∈ Haws we define un := an T n f . Then with C := supn∈N |an | we have

               1 N                   1 N                        
                 ∑
               N n=1
                     ( un+k | un ) =   ∑
                                     N n=1
                                           an+k an T n+k f T n f

                                               1 N  k               
                                       ≤ C2      ∑
                                               N n=1
                                                     T f f = C2 T k f f .

So the averages (21.1) converge to 0 by the van der Corput Lemma 9.28.
To prove (iv) ⇒ (ii), we take an isometry T on a Hilbert space H. By the JdLG-
decomposition, see Section 16.3, it suffices to prove convergence of the weighted
averages for f ∈ Hrev and f ∈ Haws separately. By the previous paragraph we know
convergence to 0 on Haws . If f is an eigenvector to some eigenvalue λ (necessarily
unimodular), then
                                             1 N
                            AN,(an ) [T ] f = ∑ an λ n f .
                                             N n=1



Published: Graduate Text in Mathematics, vol. 272, Springer-Verlag, 2015.
21.1 Weighted Ergodic Theorems                                                     431

So by assumption (iv) and by Theorem 16.33 we obtain convergence on Hrev , hence
on H, and the formula (21.3) in the case of isometries.
Finally, we prove the implication (ii) ⇒ (i) and the formula (21.3) for contractions.
Let T be a contraction on a Hilbert space H. By the Foiaş–Szőkefalvi-Nagy de-
composition in Section D.7, one has the orthogonal decomposition H = Huni ⊕ Hcnu
into two T -invariant subspaces, where T is unitary on Huni and completely nonuni-
tary and weakly stable on Hcnu , i.e., the powers T n restricted to Hcnu converge to
0 in the weak operator topology. By (ii) and by the already proven formula (21.3)
for isometries, we may assume that H = Hcnu . In this case we need to prove that
AN,(an ) [T ] f → 0 for every f ∈ H as N → ∞. By the Szőkefalvi-Nagy dilation the-
orem in Section D.8 there is a Hilbert space K ⊇ H and a unitary operator U on K
such that T n = PH U n |H holds for every n ∈ N. Since the weighted ergodic averages
converge for U by assumption, they also converge for T . It remains only to show that
the limit (21.3) is zero. Since T is weakly stable, the operators Sn := an T n converge
weakly to 0 as n → ∞, and we obtain that

                                                 1 N
                                                   ∑ Sn f
                                                 N n=1

converges weakly hence strongly to 0 for every f ∈ H.
An alternative proof for unitary operators based on the spectral theorem is Exercise
1.
Remarks 21.3. 1) One can show that (iii) implies that c(λ ) 6= 0 holds for at
most countably many λ ∈ T, see (Kahane 1985, p. 72) or Boshernitzan’s proof in
(Rosenblatt 1994). Moreover, the assertion of Theorem 21.2 can be generalized to
some classes of unbounded sequences (an )n∈N , see (Berend et al. 2002) and (Lin et
al. 1999) for details.
  2) Again using the JdLG-decomposition, see Section 16.3, one can add another
equivalent condition to the list in Theorem 21.2:
  (v) For every operator T with relatively (strongly) compact orbits on a Banach
      space E, the averages (21.1) converge strongly/weakly for every f ∈ E, and
      the limit is as given in (21.3). Here, Pλ denotes the mean ergodic projection
      of the operator λ T for λ ∈ T and the sum on the right hand side of (21.3)
      becomes for fixed f a strongly convergent series.
Note that for such operators, T n converges strongly to 0 on Eaws .
  3) We see that only the reversible part of Hrev contributes to the limit in (21.3).
Therefore, for Koopman operators the Kronecker factor is characteristic for aver-
ages (21.3), cf. page 418 in Chapter 20.
  4) By considering rotation systems (T, m; λ ) for λ ∈ T we can formulate one
more condition equivalent to the ones in Theorem 21.2.
 (vi) For every measure-preserving system (X; ϕ) with Koopman operator T := Tϕ
      the weighted averages AN,(an ) [T ] f converge in L2 for every f ∈ L2 (X).

Example 21.4. As example of good weights we can take polynomial sequences of
the form
                       
         an n∈N = λ q(n) n∈N with λ ∈ T and q : Z → Z a polynomial,

Analogously, one defines (universally) good weights for the pointwise ergodic
theorem on Lp , p ∈ [1, ∞), as weights (an )n∈N for which the averages AN,(an ) [T ] f
converge a.e. for the Koopman operator T := Tϕ of every measure-preserving sys-
tem (X; ϕ), and every f ∈ Lp (X). There seems to be no pointwise analogue of The-
orem 21.2.
   For an extension of Birkhoff’s pointwise ergodic theorem for weights coming
from orbits of measure-preserving systems see Theorem 21.10 and the discussion
below, and for more examples of pointwise good and bad (i.e., not good) weights
see, e.g., Section 21.4 below, (Conze 1973), (Bellow and Losert 1985) or (Kren-
gel 1971).



21.2 Wiener–Wintner and Return Time Theorems

In this section we study sequences of weights coming from a measure-preserving
system, i.e., having the form (an )n∈N = ( f (ϕ n (x)))n∈N for a system (X; ϕ), x ∈ X
and f ∈ L∞ (X). We will see that for almost every x such weights are good for both
the mean and the pointwise ergodic theorem.
We begin with the following classical result due to Wiener and Wintner (1941)
showing almost everywhere convergence of weighted ergodic averages with weights
an = λ n , λ ∈ T.

Theorem 21.5 (Wiener–Wintner). Let (X; ϕ), X = (X, Σ , µ), be a measure-
preserving system and f ∈ L1 (X). Then there exists a set X 0 ∈ Σ with µ(X 0 ) = 1
such that
                               1 N n            
                                  ∑
                               N n=1
                                     λ f ϕ n (x)                           (21.4)

converges for every x ∈ X 0 and λ ∈ T.

At the first glance, the coefficients (λ n )n∈N in (21.4) can be considered as a sequence
of weights. However, we can change perspective and consider instead the sequence
(an )n∈N := ( f (ϕ n (x)))n∈N as a weight. With this point of view the averages (21.4)
coincide with those in (21.2) in Theorem 21.2. We thus immediately obtain the
following corollary relating Theorems 21.2 and 21.5.
Corollary 21.6. Let (X; ϕ) be a measure-preserving system and f ∈ L∞ (X). Then
for almost every x the sequence of weights ( f (ϕ n (x)))n∈N is good for the mean
ergodic theorem.


Published: Graduate Text in Mathematics, vol. 272, Springer-Verlag, 2015.
21.2 Wiener–Wintner and Return Time Theorems                                             433

The almost everywhere convergence of (21.4) for a fixed λ ∈ T follows from
Birkhoff’s Theorem 11.1 applied to the product system (Y, ν; ψ) and g ∈ L1 (Y, ν)
for Y := T × X with product measure ν, ψ(z, x) := (λ z, φ (x)) and g(z, x) := z f (x).
The difficulty is to find a set X 0 of full measure independent of λ ∈ T.
For the proof of Theorem 21.5 we first need a simple lemma responsible for a
density argument. Here, for an ergodic measure-preserving system (X; ϕ), X =
(X, Σ , µ) and an integrable function f on X we call a point x ∈ X generic for f
if

an ergodic measure-preserving system (X; ϕ) and f ∈ L1 (X) almost every point is
generic for f .

We now prove the Wiener–Wintner theorem under the additional assumption that
the system (X; ϕ) is ergodic.
Proof of Theorem 21.5 for ergodic systems. In the whole proof we work with arbi-
trarily chosen representatives instead of equivalence classes in L2 , still denoted by
the same letter. Let H := L2 (X), T := Tϕ be the corresponding Koopman-operator,
and consider the JdLG-decomposition H = Hrev ⊕ Haws , see Section 16.3. We first
prove convergence of (21.4) for f in the reversible part Hrev . Let f be an eigenfunc-
tion of T for an eigenvalue ν ∈ T. Then there is a set Xν ∈ Σ with full measure such

                              1 N n                1 N

                              N n=1

                                                   N n=1

and convergence follows for every λ ∈ T. Clearly, if f is a finite sum of eigen-
functions corresponding to unimodular eigenvalues, then the asserted convergence
holds.
Let now f = lim j→∞ f j in L2 , where each f j is a finite sum of eigenfunctions corre-
sponding to unimodular eigenvalues. There are only countably many eigenfunctions
gi that occur as a summand in any of the functions f j . Let X 0 be the intersection of
the sets of convergence corresponding to each gi obtained from the previous argu-
ment together with the generic points of each | f j | and | f − f j |. This set is of full
measure, and from Lemma 21.7 one obtains the convergence of the averages in
(21.4).
Suppose now that f ∈ Haws . Define X 0 to be the set of the generic points of every
function T k f · f , k ∈ N. We show that the limit of (21.4) is 0 for all x ∈ X 0 and all
λ ∈ T using the van der Corput lemma. We take x ∈ X 0 and set un = λ n f (ϕ n (x)) for

for every λ ∈ T finishing the argument in case f ∈ Haws .
If f ∈ L∞ (X) is arbitrary, then its reversible and stable parts frev and faws both belong

   As we see from the proof, only functions from the reversible part contribute to
the limit of (21.4), or, in other words, the Kronecker factor is characteristic for the
Wiener–Wintner ergodic averages. In fact, one has even stronger convergence on
the stable part, as the following extension due to Bourgain (1990) shows, see also
(Assani 2003, Thms. 2.4, 2.10).
Theorem 21.8 (Uniform Wiener–Wintner Theorem). Let T be a Koopman op-

In particular, in the latter case the sequence ( f (ϕ n (x)))n∈N is a good weight for the

The proof is analogous to the one of Theorem 21.5 using a finitary version of the
van der Corput lemma, see, e.g., (Assani 2003, Ch. 2) and (Schreiber 2013a).

of weights see (Lesigne 1990, Lesigne 1993), (Frantzikinakis 2006), (Host and

   We also refer to (Lenz 2009b) for the connection of topological Wiener–Wintner

sults are in (Robinson 1994), (Lenz 2009b, Lenz 2009a), (Walters 1996), (Santos
